title: 国家发改委发布“一老一小”服务体系建设实施方案图解

title: 国家发改委刊发专家解读：织牢织密养老育幼服务网 托举“一老一小”民生福祉
originalTitle: 专家解读文章 | 织牢织密养老育幼服务网 托举“一老一小”民生福祉
summary: 国家发改委网站刊发专家解读文章，聚焦织牢织密养老育幼服务网、托举“一老一小”民生福祉。文章围绕养老、育幼服务体系建设这一民生重点展开解读，属部委层面的政策解读内容。
source: 国家发改委 · 政策通知
context: “一老一小”是民生保障重点领域，部委网站的专家解读有助于把握养老育幼服务体系的政策取向。
contentHtml:
人口问题是“国之大者”，“一老一小”是民生关切。习近平总书记指出，让老年人老有所养、生活幸福、健康长寿是我们的共同愿望；孩子们成长得更好，是我们最大的心愿。健全养老育幼服务体系，增进“一老一小”民生福祉，既是赓续中华民族敬老爱幼的传统美德，也是坚持人民至上理念的生动实践。当前，我国人口发展呈现老龄化、少子化、区域人口增减分化的趋势性特征，加快构建覆盖全人群、全生命周期的人口服务体系的必要性和紧迫性更加凸显。近日，经国务院同意，国家发展改革委等部门联合印发《“一老一小”服务体系建设实施方案》，围绕优化资源布局、提升服务品质、完善管理模式、健全保障措施等方面提出明确的工作任务和目标要求，为“十五五”时期“一老一小”服务体系建设提供了“任务书”和“施工图”。

　　一、优化资源布局，增强服务设施可及性、便利性

　　近年来，我国养老育幼服务体系建设取得积极进展，服务设施网络进一步健全。2025年末，全国养老机构和设施39.5万个，养老床位767.9万张；托育机构12.6万家，千人口托位数达到4.73个。但随着人口结构和分布变化，满足家门口普惠便利的养老育幼服务需求还面临不少瓶颈制约。

　　《实施方案》立足未来一段时期人口发展变化和需求升级趋势，从养老服务设施规划布局、医养结合有序扩容、健全托育服务网络、推进设施功能整合和公共环境改造四个方面提出资源优化布局的思路举措。优化养老服务设施规划布局方面，提出要科学规划、合理布局养老服务网络，重点推进建成时间较长、设施老旧的2000个公办养老机构改造升级，有序推进乡镇（街道）区域养老服务中心建设，统筹盘活用好乡村小型互助养老服务设施。到2030年，养老机构护理型养老床位占比将达到73%，社区养老服务机构和设施覆盖率将达到70%。医养结合有序扩容方面，结合本地实际需求适当支持二级及以下医疗卫生机构发展医养结合服务，支持有条件的地方毗邻医疗卫生机构规划建设养老服务机构，实现医养服务有效衔接。完善托育服务设施网络方面，加快实现地市级托育综合服务中心全覆盖，支持有条件的幼儿园举办面向2—3岁幼儿的托班，在人口较多的农村设置托育点等。到2030年，3岁以下婴幼儿入托率较2025年将提高6个百分点。设施功能整合和公共环境改造方面，重点将推动社区嵌入式服务设施集成老年人和婴幼儿日间照料、休闲娱乐等多样化功能，发展半日托、计时托等服务，规范发展“老幼共托”模式。同时，还将推进公共场所、交通运输设施适老化、适儿化和无障碍改造，打造老年友好、儿童友好社会环境。

　　二、提升服务质量，满足多样化、高品质服务需求

　　老有所养、幼有善育是人民群众的迫切期盼，“一老一小”服务正在变为千家万户的“刚性需求”。在扩大服务设施供给的同时，服务质量成为影响设施利用率的重要因素。当前，人民群众对养老育幼的需求越来越大，对服务优质和价格普惠的期待越来越高，要求养老、托育服务设施加快向普惠化、品质化转变。

　　《实施方案》聚焦提升养老育幼服务品质，提出健全标准规范体系、扩大普惠服务供给、积极发展多样化服务、深入推进科技赋能等四方面“软建设”配套举措。标准规范方面，提出加快修订完善老年养护院、托育机构、托育综合服务中心相关建设标准或规范，健全养老、托育领域服务标准，逐步推行老年人能力评估、失能老年人健康评估、长期护理失能等级评估、残疾分类和分级等评估“多评合一”。普惠服务供给方面，制定完善普惠养老价格政策，完善普惠托育服务价格形成机制，落实普惠养老、托育机构相关税收、水电气热价格优惠政策，鼓励有条件的地方结合实际为普惠养老、托育机构给予稳定可预期的运营补贴，将符合条件的幼儿园托班纳入普惠托育补贴范围，引导各类主体积极参与提供普惠服务。发展多样化服务方面，提出依托养老机构，贯通衔接居家和社区养老服务，为失能失智、独居老人等困难群体提供助餐、助洁、助浴等上门服务。积极发展老年人心理健康关爱服务、托育健康指导服务。依托托育综合服务中心、妇幼保健机构等，为家庭提供儿童早期发展指导服务，多渠道扩大服务资源供给。科技赋能方面，支持养老、托育机构应用智能管理、智慧消防安防系统，推动养老机构配置智能健康监测、辅助器具等设备。鼓励发展适合养老场景的人工智能体、服务机器人、智能穿戴设备、外骨骼等新产品。

　　三、完善管理模式，赋能养老育幼高质量发展

　　养老、托育服务涉及民政、卫生健康、教育、消防救援等多部门，跨部门管理协调事项多，需要做好相关政策的统筹衔接。在推动“一老一小”服务从“强供给”向“优适配”转变的同时，也需要进一步完善管理机制，吸引社会力量参与，赋能养老育幼行业高质量发展。

　　《实施方案》围绕提升城乡统筹水平、创新管理运营模式、健全协同管理制度等三个方面提出创新举措。城乡统筹方面，提出以地市为单位整体谋划推进养老服务、医养结合、托育服务发展，推动设施和服务向常住人口密集、需求旺盛的地区倾斜。运营模式方面，探索构建城乡养老服务联合体，发挥托育综合服务中心示范带动作用，支持采取购买服务、公建民营、民办公助等方式吸引专业化社会力量参与，促进连锁化、品牌化运营。协同管理方面，支持各地结合实际加强医养结合、幼儿园办托等领域跨部门协同管理，定期协商解决日常监管、政策衔接等问题。民政、卫生健康部门根据医养结合服务提供机构性质，按照职能职责分工开展日常监管。教育部门加强幼儿园托班规划布局、举办条件把关，卫生健康部门对幼儿园托班进行备案管理和业务指导。

　　四、加强保障支撑，夯实“一老一小”民生福祉

　　“一老一小”事关亿万家庭福祉和国家长远发展，需要各地区、各有关部门齐抓共管，统筹用好各类资金渠道，健全综合监管体系，共同支撑“一老一小”服务体系建设和可持续运营。《实施方案》从加大要素支持、强化综合监管方面提出具体工作要求。加大要素支持方面，提出加强资金、用地、人才保障，统筹用好中央预算内投资、地方自有财力和政府专项债券等资金渠道支持设施建设和可持续运营，保障养老、托育服务设施合理用地需求，健全专业人员培训体系，完善薪酬待遇、职称评定等激励机制，支持职业院校与养老、托育机构开展实训合作。强化综合监管方面，提出督促指导养老、托育机构制定突发事件应急预案，定期组织安全防护演练，依法依规追究安全事故责任，强化价格收费监督检查，完善养老、托育机构信用评价与失信惩戒机制，切实保护好“一老一小”群体各项权益。

　　老吾老以及人之老，幼吾幼以及人之幼。养老育幼牵动千家万户，涉及资源配置、服务质量、管理机制、要素保障等方方面面，唯有统筹施策、久久为功，不断完善“一老一小”服务体系建设，把群众关切的“小事”办成可感可及的“实事”，才能更好满足人民群众对美好生活向往，托举起“夕阳红”“朝阳艳”的幸福生活。（国家发展改革委国家信息中心副研究员  韩瑞栋）

title: 人社部：非法骗取社保基金支出或社保待遇 拟处骗取金额2倍以上5倍以下罚款
originalTitle: 人社部：非法骗取社保基金支出或者社保待遇 拟处骗取金额2倍以上5倍以下的罚款
summary: 人社部研究起草的《社会保险基金监督条例（征求意见稿）》向社会公开征求意见，拟对以欺诈、伪造证明材料等手段骗取社保基金支出或待遇者，责令退回骗取的社会保险金并处骗取金额2倍以上5倍以下罚款。属社保服务机构的将解除服务协议，直接负责的主管人员和其他直接责任人员有执业资格的依法吊销执业资格。
context: 社保基金监管拟增设明确罚则，欺诈骗保违法成本显著提高，关系广大参保人与服务机构权益。
contentHtml:
人力资源社会保障部研究起草了《社会保险基金监督条例（征求意见稿）》，现向社会公开征求意见。意见稿提出，有下列情形之一，以欺诈、伪造证明材料或者其他手段骗取社会保险基金支出或者社会保险待遇的，由人力资源社会保障行政部门责令退回骗取的社会保险金，处骗取金额2倍以上5倍以下的罚款；属于社会保险服务机构的，解除服务协议，直接负责的主管人员和其他直接责任人员有执业资格的，依法吊销其执业资格：

　　（一）伪造、变造证明材料的；

　　（二）冒用他人身份或者证件的；

　　（三）隐瞒丧失领取社会保险待遇条件的；

　　（四）虚构事实或者作出虚假承诺的；

　　（五）骗取社会保险基金支出或者社会保险待遇的其他情形。

　　有前款规定的情形，但社会保险基金尚未支出的，停止办理或者撤销相关业务；情节严重的，由人力资源社会保障行政部门处1000元以上1万元以下的罚款。

（文章来源：财联社）

title: PandaAI 完成三轮融资，99后创业者用AI打造交易者智能管家

contentHtml:
初见李不白，很难立刻把他和一家完成三轮融资的AI创业公司创始人联系起来。

他常年穿着公司的工服，春夏是短袖、卫衣，到了秋冬，觉得衣服不够穿了，就让公司再做一批外套。背着的也是一个旧双肩包。这个背包，他从高中一直背到现在。对他来说，它不只是一件用了很多年的旧物，也承载着过去那些不太容易的日子。每次看到它，都会提醒自己保持谨慎思考、独立判断，做好风险控制，同时也要在机会出现时敢于抓住。

李不白是重庆人，喜欢熊猫，也和很多二十多岁的年轻人一样，喜欢超级英雄，尤其是钢铁侠。PandaAI的Logo就是他自己设计的：把熊猫和钢铁侠头盔结合在一起。这个名字和形象也藏着他对产品的想象——像钢铁侠身边的Jarvis一样，为交易者做一个AI智能管家。而现在，用户在PandaAI里，可以用自然语言提出一个投资研究问题。平台内嵌的模型可以调用数据、代码和回测工具，协助分析数据、研究指标、验证策略。但最后怎么判断、怎么交易，仍由用户自己决定。

01 从交易到科普：让更多人看懂量化

99年出生的李不白，20岁便进入量化私募行业，曾参与管理规模超过10亿元的资金。最初选择交易，并不完全出于对金融行业的职业规划。家庭等现实因素，让他很早就需要考虑如何赚钱。

问他为什么喜欢交易，他给出的答案是：“交易的另外一个名字应该叫做决策。”在真实的市场里，人需要不断作出判断，而结果很快就会反馈回来。一次选择是否有效，不必反复猜测，市场会给出回应。这种快速判断、快速反馈的过程，正是吸引他的地方。

李不白活动图片

参与私募业务期间，李不白开始运营自媒体账号“量化李不白”。起初的想法很简单：他发现大众对量化投资存在很大的信息差。量化常常被描述成一种神秘、复杂，甚至与普通投资者对立的力量。李不白不太认同这种说法。在他看来，量化首先是一种研究方法，背后有具体的逻辑和技术，不应该因为涉及数学、统计和编程，就成为只有少数专业人士才能理解的黑箱。

他希望把这些知识讲清楚，让更多人知道量化究竟在做什么。对李不白来说，科普的意义也不只是消除误解，而是让知识和技术有机会流动起来，专业能力不应该只掌握在少数拥有资源和门槛的人手里。于是，他开始持续更新内容，讲量化策略、研究方法和相关技术。账号逐渐积累了20多万粉丝，但随之而来的也有不解：既然在做私募，何必花精力搞自媒体？甚至连部分股东和客户也觉得，这偏离了原本的业务方向。

李不白还是继续做了下去。他看到的是量化领域长期存在的信息差，以及信息差背后真实的知识需求。随着内容传播，粉丝提出的问题也开始发生变化：听懂了方法之后，能不能真正用起来？有没有工具帮助自己做因子研究、写策略、分析数据？这些反馈让他意识到，用户需要的不只是知识，还需要把知识变成实践的工具。

这成为他创业的起点。早期的粉丝和开源社区，也成为PandaAI最初的一批用户。从量化私募到自媒体，再到AI产品创业，李不白并不是一开始就奔着创办一家科技公司去的。他的路径更像是被一个个具体问题推着往前走：先是因为交易进入量化领域，后来发现很多人不了解量化，于是开始做科普；再后来，粉丝不满足于听懂知识，而是希望拥有能够亲自使用的工具。PandaAI就这样一步步出现了。

PandaAI官网界面

02 从一个工具到一支Agent团队

大模型出现后，李不白开始思考，AI能不能进一步降低量化研究的门槛。团队最初尝试用Coding Agent帮用户写代码、开发策略和做回测，但很快发现，会写代码不等于会交易。一个交易者真正要完成的研究任务，往往涉及数据搜集、因子挖掘、策略构建、回测验证和风险分析。只解决代码生成，远远不够。

PandaAI因此逐渐从单点工具转向完整的AI投研工作流。用户可以通过自然语言描述研究想法，由AI调用数据、模型、代码和回测工具，协助完成投资研究的任务。量化用户可以用它做因子研究和策略开发，主观投资者则可以用它分析研报、搜集数据和整理信息。团队希望帮助用户完成研究，而不是直接给出买卖建议，最终的投资判断和交易决定，仍然掌握在用户自己手中。PandaAI从写代码扩展到投研流程，就是为了帮助用户把这些环节接起来，把听懂的方法用到自己的研究里。

李不白活动图片

但自然语言交互并不是他设想中的终点。李不白更期待下一代产品走向A2A，也就是Agent-to-Agent的协作模式。他把它想象成一个“A2A 办公室”：用户可以根据自己的投资理念和研究习惯，选择不同能力的Agent，组成自己的 Agent团队。不同Agent分别承担数据处理、因子研究、策略分析等工作，彼此协作完成一项投研任务。

这意味着，AI不再只是等待指令、完成单项任务的工具，而是逐渐参与到研究过程之中。不同Agent可以根据用户的反馈和新的研究结果调整方法，形成一套持续迭代的工作体系。

这种对产品形态的想象，也和李不白对公司的期待有关。他不希望PandaAI成为一家沿用传统金融行业表达方式的公司。金融行业过去给人的印象往往严肃、专业，甚至有些距离感。他希望PandaAI从一开始就代表另一种气质：年轻、技术驱动，愿意用新的技术范式重新进入一个古老的行业。

03 三轮融资之后，他仍然在学习怎么创业

PandaAI正式开启外部融资后，在两个月内连续完成种子轮、天使轮和天使+轮融资，累计融资数千万元人民币，由L2F光源创业者基金领投。资金将用于AI交易大模型、专业QuantSkills、多智能体协作基础设施和交易Agent开发环境等方向，进一步推进PandaAI OS、EVO和A2A技术体系建设。

比起一个已经完成三轮融资的创业公司创始人，李不白身上更明显的特质，是不设边界的求知欲和持续学习的能力。过去积累的金融、统计和编程知识，为他进入量化行业打下了基础。而无论是早期做交易，还是后来投身AI创业，李不白始终保持着很强的学习欲望。从AI技术、模型和Agent，到公司管理、商务和运营，他都在不断拓展自己的知识边界。对他来说，创业过程中遇到什么问题，就去学习解决这个问题所需要的东西。

他不太愿意依赖过去的经验给自己设限，也不认为做过金融就只能沿着金融行业的老路走。团队成员评价他行动力很强，想到一个方向，通常不会停留在讨论上，而是会着手研究、尝试落地。至于结果如何，再根据实际反馈调整。这种先行动、再学习、再迭代的方式，也贯穿了他从交易、自媒体到AI创业的经历。

李不白活动图片

李不白认为，过去二十年，优秀交易员依靠经验和研究创造Alpha。未来二十年，Agent也会参与其中。人与人之间的竞争仍会存在，不同Agent、不同研究体系之间，也会展开新的竞争。PandaAI想做的，是把可信数据、金融工具、Skills、Agent和投研流程连接起来，让AI不只执行任务，也能发现规律、验证结果，并不断调整研究方法。

从最初做量化科普，到今天创建PandaAI，李不白想解决的始终是同一个问题：怎么让更多人获得科学投资的专业能力。过去，他通过内容让更多人理解量化。现在，他希望借助AI，把曾经只属于少数专业机构的能力，变成更多人能够接触和使用的工具。

李不白和他的书包

那个常穿公司工服、背着高中旧书包，喜欢打游戏、听歌，养着三猫一狗的年轻人，看着钢铁侠，也曾对Jarvis这样的AI助手充满想象。如今，他正试着把这样的想象变成现实。

让AI学会如何研究，让专业投研能力不再只属于少数人。

这是PandaAI想要实现的愿景，也是李不白用代码写下的，属于自己的超级英雄梦。

关于PandaAI ：

PandaAI是国内首个AI金融投研基础设施平台，为个人或机构提供一站式AI量化投资研究解决方案。通过自然语言和可视化工作流连接交易想法到策略、回测、执行的全流程，让不会写代码的人也能把自己的市场判断走完从研究到验证的全过程。目前海内外用户已超过15万，在两个月内连续完成种子轮、天使轮及天使+轮三轮融资，由L2F光源创业者基金领投，估值超千万元人民币。

title: 韩国教育部长崔教振辞职，称年事已高难以应对AI考试作弊问题
originalTitle: 韩国教育部长辞职，称自己年事已高难以应对AI考试作弊问题。
summary: 韩国教育部长崔教振辞职，其自称年事已高，难以应对大学入学考试中的AI作弊问题。此前，韩国政府在采取措施打击该国竞争激烈的大学入学考试中利用AI作弊的行为时陷入混乱。
source: 新浪财经 · 实时滚动
context: 事件折射出AI对传统考试制度与教育治理的直接冲击，在韩国高考竞争激烈的背景下具有政策信号意义。

title: 智谱GLM-5.4上线：首款Loop架构国产旗舰模型，3万亿参数GLM-5.5预计12月发布
summary: 智谱GLM-5.4今日中午上线Coding Plan订阅体系，官方尚未正式发布，该模型采用Loop Transformer架构，是国内首款基于该架构的旗舰模型。内测用户反馈其综合表现优于3万亿参数级别的Kimi K3.1 Pro，官方跑分暂未公布。智谱管理层预计四季度推出约3万亿参数旗舰模型，市场普遍预期GLM-5.5于12月接力发布。
context: 智谱旗舰迭代节奏明显加快，Loop新架构与3万亿参数升级双线推进，是观察国产大模型竞争格局的关键节点。
contentHtml:
记者获悉，智谱GLM-5.4于今日中午上线Coding Plan订阅体系，官方尚未正式发布。另据智谱官方社群消息，GLM-5.4采用Loop Transformer架构，是国内首款基于该架构的旗舰模型。内测用户反馈其综合表现优于3万亿级别参数的Kimi K3.1 Pro，官方跑分暂未公布。

据了解，智谱管理层预计四季度推出约3万亿参数的旗舰模型，市场普遍预期是GLM-5.5于12月接力发布。（澎湃）

title: 三星首款AI智能眼镜将于12月10日在韩国和美国发布
originalTitle: 三星首款人工智能眼镜将于下月10日发布
summary: 三星电子将于12月10日在韩国和美国推出其首款AI智能眼镜。该眼镜支持基于Gemini的翻译、导航和会议摘要功能。
context: 三星作为消费电子巨头首次入局AI眼镜赛道，并深度整合谷歌Gemini能力，是AI硬件落地的标志性动向。

title: 钟南山谈AI：医疗健康领域必须有专业AI，医学容不得半点"差不多"
originalTitle: 钟南山谈AI：医疗健康领域必须有专业AI 医学容不得半点“差不多”
summary: 11月23日，中国工程院院士钟南山在2026蚂蚁阿福医疗健康生态大会上表示，医疗健康领域必须有专业的医学AI。他认为AI可以成为守护居民健康的温暖力量，让更多老百姓看得上病、看得好病、看得明白病，但医学容不得半点"差不多"。当前医生、患者使用AI已成为大趋势。
context: 在医生与患者使用AI渐成趋势之际，钟南山对医学AI专业性提出明确要求，对AI医疗行业具有风向意义。

title: 国际金价低位反弹，美债收益率回落缓解金价下行压力
originalTitle: 今日黄金：低位反弹，美债收益率回落缓解金价下行压力
summary: 11月23日，国际金价在连续五个交易日下跌后反弹，结束此前抛售行情。此前跌势源于市场流动性紧张、美元走强及美联储加息预期升温。随着美国国债收益率回落，黄金持有成本下降，金价下行压力有所缓解。
source: 新浪财经 · 实时滚动
context: 金价走势与美元、美债收益率及美联储政策预期高度联动，此番止跌反弹可作为观察贵金属短期方向的重要信号。

title: 康菲石油拟以44.25亿美元向VrEnergi出售挪威业务及英国蒂赛德油码头权益
originalTitle: 康菲石油拟以44.25亿美元出售挪威业务及英国蒂赛德油码头权益
summary: 美国康菲石油11月23日宣布，已与挪威油气企业VrEnergi达成最终协议，拟以44.25亿美元出售其挪威业务及英国蒂赛德（Teesside）油码头40.25%股权与运营权。交易对价需扣除截至2026年1月1日生效日约5亿美元的约定调整款。交易预计2027年一季度末前完成，尚需挪威能源部批准并满足相关监管条件。
context: 康菲石油借此交易整体剥离挪威资产，是国际油气巨头资产组合调整中规模较大的剥离案例。

title: 特朗普再次公开呼吁英伟达董事会重新聘用前CEO黄仁勋
originalTitle: 最大科技多头发力：特朗普再次呼吁英伟达董事会重新聘用黄仁勋
summary: 11月23日，美国总统特朗普再次公开呼吁英伟达董事会重新聘用前首席执行官黄仁勋，称其回归将同时符合英伟达及美国的利益。此前，英伟达董事会已明确表示不会重新聘用黄仁勋。
source: 新浪财经 · 实时滚动
context: 总统公开为芯片巨头前CEO回归喊话、董事会明确拒绝，双方分歧走向对英伟达后续发展具有风向意义。
contentHtml:
11月23日，美国总统特朗普再次公开呼吁英伟达董事会重新聘用前首席执行官黄仁勋，称其回归将同时符合英伟达及美国的利益。此前，英伟达董事会已明确表示不会重新聘用黄仁勋，并启动新任首席执行官遴选程序。英伟达董事长哈维·琼斯（Harvey Jones）上周明确表示，公司不会重新聘用黄仁勋，并已聘请高管猎头公司Heidrick & Struggles协助寻找新任首席执行官。

　　特朗普在Truth Social平台发文称：“我希望英伟达董事会重新聘用黄仁勋。这对公司和美国而言都将是最好的选择。”

　　这是特朗普继黄仁勋11月12日辞职后，再次公开支持其重返英伟达。此前，特朗普曾表示，黄仁勋已经吸取教训，理应获得第二次机会。

title: 必和必拓计划2040年前将南澳铜产量翻倍至65万吨，股价涨超2%
summary: 全球最大上市铜生产商必和必拓（BHP）11月23日宣布，计划到2040年将其南澳大利亚铜业务年产量翻倍至65万吨，以满足电气化、可再生能源及人工智能发展推动的长期铜需求。消息公布后，公司股价涨超2%。
source: 新浪财经 · 实时滚动
context: AI与能源转型持续推升铜需求，全球最大铜生产商的长期扩产计划对铜供需格局和矿业板块具有风向标意义。
contentHtml:
11月23日，全球最大上市铜生产商必和必拓（BHP）宣布，计划到2040年将旗下南澳大利亚铜业务的年产量翻倍至65万吨，以满足电气化、可再生能源及人工智能发展推动的长期铜需求增长。

　　消息公布后，截至发稿，必和必拓澳大利亚上市股票上涨约2.3%，报52.6澳元。

　　2035年集团铜产量目标为200万吨

　　根据必和必拓在投资者演示会上公布的扩产计划，公司拟将集团应占铜年产量从目前约140万吨提升至2035年的200万吨，增幅约43%。

　　其中，南澳大利亚铜业务预计将贡献集团2035年前计划新增铜产量的约三分之一。

　　南澳铜业务扩产将分两个阶段实施：

  • 第一阶段：将铜年产量提升至约50万吨。

  • 第二阶段：进一步将年产量提升至65万吨，计划于2040年前实现。

　　预计铜业务2035年前累计产生350亿美元自由现金流

　　必和必拓表示，南澳铜业务扩产所需资金将主要来自铜业务自身的经营现金流。

　　公司预计，截至2035年，旗下铜业务累计将产生约350亿美元的应占自由现金流，为产能扩张提供资金支持。

　　在长期需求方面，必和必拓认为，全球电气化、可再生能源投资、数字化转型及人工智能基础设施建设将持续推动铜需求增长。

　　该公司同时警告，现有铜矿的供应能力不足以满足未来市场需求，全球铜产业仍需扩大投资及新增产能，以应对长期供需缺口。

title: 国家发改委等四部门印发《“一老一小”服务体系建设实施方案》
originalTitle: 国家发展改革委 民政部 国家卫生健康委 教育部印发《“一老一小”服务体系建设实施方案》
summary: 国家发展改革委、民政部、国家卫生健康委、教育部四部门联合印发《“一老一小”服务体系建设实施方案》。方案聚焦养老与儿童服务两大民生领域，由四部委协同部署推进。
source: 国家发改委 · 政策通知
context: “一老一小”是重点民生议题，四部委联合发文显示顶层协同推进力度，养老、托育相关产业值得关注。
contentHtml:
为深入贯彻落实党中央、国务院关于促进人口高质量发展的决策部署，扩大养老、托育服务有效供给，日前，经国务院同意，国家发展改革委、民政部、国家卫生健康委、教育部印发《“一老一小”服务体系建设实施方案》（以下简称《实施方案》）。

　　《实施方案》要求，坚持以习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想为指导，深入贯彻党的二十大和二十届历次全会精神，坚持以人民为中心的发展思想，坚持因地制宜、分级分类，坚持改革创新、系统集成，坚持投资于物和投资于人紧密结合，统筹发展和安全，统筹推进“硬投资”与“软建设”，着力完善设施、提升服务、增强效能，提高养老、托育服务供给与人民群众需求的适配度，加快构建更加适应人口结构变化的“一老一小”服务体系。

　　《实施方案》明确，到2030年，养老、托育服务设施布局更加合理、条件明显改善，医养结合持续深化，“一老一小”服务体系进一步健全、供需适配度进一步提高，养老机构护理型床位占比达到73%，社区养老服务机构和设施覆盖率达到70%，3岁以下婴幼儿入托率较2025年提高6个百分点，覆盖城乡、布局合理、价格可接受、质量有保障的普惠养老、托育服务供给格局基本形成。

　　《实施方案》提出，在优化资源布局方面，将根据常住人口规模、结构、分布变化和流动趋势等，加强养老服务设施规划布局，推动医养结合服务设施有序扩容，健全托育服务设施网络，推进设施功能整合和公共环境改造，加快完善服务设施体系。在提升服务品质方面，将加快健全养老、托育领域服务标准和建设规范，完善价格机制，积极拓展多样化服务，加快智能技术在养老、托育领域落地应用，更好满足群众需求。在完善管理模式方面，将推动设施和服务向人口密集、需求旺盛的县乡村倾斜，探索构建城乡养老服务联合体，发挥托育综合服务中心示范带动作用，理顺医养结合、幼儿园办托管理机制，切实增强服务效能。在健全保障措施方面，将加大资金、土地、人才等要素支撑，加强安全、价格、信用等监督监管，更好保障“一老一小”群体基本权益，全面夯实发展基础。

　　《实施方案》强调，各地区、各有关部门要加强组织领导，结合实际落实工作责任，及时研判分析新情况、协调解决新问题，认真开展成效评估，确保“一老一小”服务体系建设取得实效。鼓励将“一老一小”服务体系建设纳入本地区经济社会发展、国土空间等相关规划和民生实事清单。国家发展改革委、民政部、国家卫生健康委、教育部加强统筹指导，总结经验做法，推动地区间、行业间交流互鉴，持续提升“一老一小”服务体系建设质效。

title: 国家发展改革委就《全国守信激励措施基础清单（2026年版）》答记者问
originalTitle: 国家发展改革委有关负责同志就《全国守信激励措施基础清单（2026年版）》答记者问
summary: 国家发展改革委有关负责同志就《全国守信激励措施基础清单（2026年版）》答记者问，对清单有关情况作出官方说明。该清单为2026年版全国层面的守信激励措施基础清单。
source: 国家发改委 · 政策通知
context: 国家发改委就全国性守信激励清单集中答问，是观察社会信用体系建设与信用激励政策走向的重要窗口。
contentHtml:
近日，国家发展改革委、中国人民银行联合印发《全国守信激励措施基础清单（2026年版）》（以下简称《激励清单》）。国家发展改革委有关负责同志就《激励清单》相关问题回答了记者提问。

　　问：出台《激励清单》的背景是什么？

　　答：习近平总书记强调，要建立和完善守信联合激励和失信联合惩戒制度，充分运用信用激励和约束手段，建立跨地区、跨部门、跨领域联合激励与惩戒机制。《中共中央办公厅、国务院办公厅关于健全社会信用体系的意见》提出，要构建全方位的信用激励政策环境。为进一步明确信用激励的认定主体、激励对象和实施方式，提升激励措施的系统性、协同性和可感性，促进形成诚信者受益的良好氛围，我们推动出台了《激励清单》。具体来说，主要有以下三方面考虑。

　　第一，弘扬诚信、厚植根基。让守信者享便利、得实惠，是全社会最生动的诚信教育。《激励清单》把“守信有价、守信有感”从理念变为可操作、可核验、可评估的具体安排，有利于营造知信、守信、用信的良好社会氛围，夯实高质量发展的信用根基。

　　第二，破除壁垒、畅通循环。社会信用制度是市场经济的基础制度之一，建设全国统一大市场需要统一的信用制度规则。以全国统一的清单规范激励措施，推动信用评价结果跨部门、跨领域互认共享，有利于破除激励政策的部门分割和地区壁垒，为商品要素资源在更大范围内畅通流动提供制度保障。

　　第三，稳定预期、提振信心。守信激励政策指向明确，信用主体切身可感。通过清单化、制度化方式，让守信企业特别是中小微企业在办事、融资、监管、交易各环节得到实实在在的便利，有利于降低制度性交易成本，增强经营主体信心，激发市场活力。

　　问：《激励清单》是如何构建联合激励机制的？

　　答：《激励清单》综合运用行政化、社会化方式，对政府部门和有关单位认定的自然人、法人和非法人组织等守信主体进行激励，围绕“谁来激励、对谁激励、如何激励、如何落实”，构建起全链条闭环管理体系。

　　一是激励主体多方参与、协同联动。《激励清单》由20个部门和单位共同编制，并联合航空、金融和互联网领域等10家企业参与实施。各方立足本单位职责职能分工配合，建立起部门协同、政企联动、社会广泛参与的守信联合激励大格局。

　　二是激励对象覆盖广泛、认定规范。《激励清单》共纳入25类守信主体，包括自然人、企事业单位、个体工商户、社会组织等各类主体，涵盖市场监管、交通运输、税务、海关、工业、生态环境等重点领域。各类主体均由有关部门依法依规认定，确保激励资源精准投放。

　　三是激励措施综合多元、精准适配。《激励清单》提出超过200项激励措施，主要分为两类。一类是行政化激励。由政府部门依据有关规定实施，主要包括荣誉表彰、宣传推广、公共信用评价加分或提升等级、适用告知承诺制、优先提供行政事项办理绿色通道、优先考虑评先评优、降低抽查检查频次等。另一类是社会化激励。由航空、金融和互联网领域企业提供，主要包括便捷乘机出行、便利金融服务、互联网平台会员权益等。《激励清单》逐项明确了激励对象、认定部门和实施主体，做到措施可执行、对象可核验。

　　四是实施路径流程闭环、便于落地。《激励清单》对细化激励方案、公开激励规则、加强信用信息归集共享和身份核验等作出安排，各项工作纳入制度化管理框架，全程可追溯、可监督，保障举措规范有序落地。

　　五是激励范围动态调整、有序拓展。《激励清单》按年度更新，将根据法律法规和政策文件调整情况及时调整激励对象和措施。同时，将推动更多部门、单位和企业加入联合激励，进一步拓展激励对象、丰富激励措施，让守信者享受到更多优惠便利。

　　问：《激励清单》在联合激励方面有什么具体举措？

　　答：联合激励的实施让“信用”成为跨部门、跨领域的通行证，为要素资源加速流动、维护全国统一大市场提供了一种低成本、可持续的治理方式。在推动联合激励方面，主要有三方面举措。

　　一是政府与市场“双轮驱动”，行政化手段和社会化措施协同供给。《激励清单》以全国统一清单的形式，把分散在各部门、各行业的守信激励措施系统集成起来，政府部门率先示范，同时广泛动员社会力量参与，形成“政府带动市场、行政撬动社会”的联合激励新格局，推动激励措施从“分散认定、各自实施”走向“联合认定、集成供给”。

　　二是激励对象跨部门共享互认，激励措施相互衔接。如纳税缴费信用A级经营主体可在认定劳动保障守法诚信A级企业时获得信用加分；海关总署为信息通信、生态环境、公路水运工程、税务、市场监管等多个领域的守信企业申请海关高级认证企业（即AEO企业）资质提供“一对一”信用培育支持，AEO企业又可同步享受生态环境、市场监管、交通运输等部门的降低检查频次、正面清单管理等便利，信用资产的“含金量”显著提升。

　　三是依托“信用+”场景落地见效，让守信可感可及。把“信易贷”“信易行”等多年探索形成的应用场景，转化为守信激励措施，推动要素资源向守信主体倾斜，真正实现“信用越好、办事越快”，让守信主体切实享受到信用红利。

　　问：如何确保《激励清单》激励措施落实落细？

　　答：为确保《激励清单》落地见效、规范实施，国家发展改革委将会同各有关方面重点抓好三方面工作。一是规范认定、强化共享。推动各认定部门（单位）严格依据有关规定开展激励对象认定，及时将名单信息推送至全国信用信息共享平台。在严格保护个人信息和商业秘密的前提下，我们将通过共享平台按程序向有关部门和企业共享。二是明确渠道、主动公开。压实参与社会化联合激励有关企业的主体责任，要求其明确申请受理条件和渠道，通过官方网站和“信用中国”网站及时向社会公布，依法依规开展激励。三是加强宣传、及时推广。会同有关部门做好政策解读和典型案例宣传，指导各地区在基础清单之上结合实际拓展激励场景、加大激励力度，及时总结推广地方经验，让守信主体应知尽知、应享尽享。

title: 运行时安全工具不等于安全基线：云原生团队中被伪装成自主性的孤岛
originalTitle: Your runtime security tool is not your baseline: Silos dressed as autonomy in cloud native teams
summary: CNCF 博客发文指出，运行时安全工具本身不能当作安全基线，云原生团队常把各自为战误当成自主性，最终形成安全孤岛。作者结合一次 Kubernetes 安全专项的经历：截止日期带来压力，一支拥有优秀工程师和清晰目标的团队决定只直接解决自己那一部分问题。
context: 文章聚焦云原生安全落地中工具定位与组织协作的常见误区，对平台与安全团队有借鉴意义。
contentHtml:
A deadline creates pressure, and a team decides to solve its part of the problem directly.

I once saw this play out in a Kubernetes security initiative. The team had capable engineers, a clear objective and a reasonable concern that asking for help might slow them down. They picked a runtime detection tool, deployed it across the clusters and had a dashboard full of events within a week.

The missing piece was not the tool. It was the baseline: the shared definition of what normal looks like for those workloads and what should be blocked rather than just reported. Without it, every alert raised the same question: is this expected? The people who could answer that sat in another team, and nobody had asked them early enough.

The decision made sense from where the team stood. They had a task, a tool and a plan. What they lacked was the cross-team agreement that makes the tool useful, and confidence that asking for it would get a timely answer.

In cloud native engineering, “we can handle this ourselves” sounds like healthy ownership, and often it is. This post is about the cases where it isn’t, and about the artifact that usually exposes the difference: the security baseline.

The new version of the silo

The old silo was a wall. The new one can be a door that closes without anyone noticing: the team keeps moving and reports progress, but a key conversation never happens.

Autonomy is not automatically a silo. A team that owns its platform and makes its own decisions is what good engineering looks like. The silo appears when autonomy turns into self-sufficiency: the team stops checking who else holds part of the answer and rebuilds knowledge that already exists elsewhere in the organisation.

Renaming a team does not fix this either. Platform security, cloud native security and DevSecOps are labels; collaboration still depends on how people work together.

Three things make the new silo likely:

  • Deadlines reward visible progress. A deployed DaemonSet and a dashboard are easy to show. Agreeing on expected behaviour, exception handling and verification is less visible, but it decides whether the deployment means anything.
  • Security looks like an approval queue. If every question to a security team turns into a review and a long wait, a well-run engineering team will reasonably try to work around it. That is a design problem for security teams, not a character flaw in platform teams.
  • Prevention is hard to measure. Shipping independently is easy to demonstrate. An early conversation that prevents rework produces a problem that never happens.

A tool working as configured is not a control

The risk is rarely that a tool fails. It is that a tool works exactly as configured, without a shared understanding of what it is supposed to achieve.

The pattern repeats across the cloud native security stack:

  • A runtime detection engine such as Falco ships with general-purpose rules. Turning its output into signal requires knowing what each workload is expected to do, and that knowledge lives with the teams that build and run those workloads.
  • An admission controller such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper can block or only report. Choosing between those modes is a risk decision, not a configuration detail.
  • Kubernetes audit logging produces evidence only if someone has decided what to record, how long to keep it and who reads it.

None of these are shortcomings of the projects. They are design dependencies: the tool provides the mechanism, and the organisation has to provide the intent.

The baseline is a cross-team artifact

A baseline is not a policy document. It is a short, testable set of answers, and every answer maps to something you can configure and verify in a cluster. The question that matters is who has to agree on each one.

A note on naming: Pod Security Standards define a profile called baseline. That profile is one useful input, but the baseline in this post is the wider organisational agreement that includes it.

Looking at the table, no single team owns every row. A platform team that deploys all of these tools alone has implemented the mechanisms and guessed at the intent. That is the new silo in its most concrete form.

Make the baseline cheap to ask about

The answer is not to send platform teams back to a security approval queue. It is to make the cross-team parts of the baseline easy to reach. Treating the baseline as code is a practical way to do that, because it uses workflows engineering teams already know:

  • Keep policies in a repository, alongside the admission policies, Falco rules and audit policy that implement them.
  • Make ownership explicit with code owners. A CODEOWNERS file can require review from security for the paths that define block-or-report decisions, and from application teams for the runtime rules that describe their workloads. Ownership stops being implicit knowledge.
  • Turn exceptions into pull requests. Each exception records the policy it bypasses, the workload it applies to, who approved it and when it expires. Expiry needs enforcement too, such as a scheduled CI check that fails when an exception has passed its date. An exception with no expiry is a permanent policy change nobody reviewed.
  • Start in report mode on purpose. Running new policies in Audit or warn first is a good practice, as long as there is an agreed date and owner for the move to enforcement. Otherwise report mode becomes the permanent state.
  • Publish a clear contact and response expectation for each owning team. A code owner who takes three weeks to review is an approval queue with better tooling.

Security teams carry half of this. When guidance is hard to find or exceptions are slow, teams have every incentive to work around the process. Autonomy is not the problem. Expensive help is.

Four decisions that rarely belong to the same person

Once a team acts, four decisions have to be made explicit:

The third row is where most programmes quietly break. The person who approves an exception must be able to fund its remediation or carry the consequence if it never happens. Someone who can sign but cannot fund is not accepting a risk. They are witnessing it.

Frameworks describe the same split. In NIST CSF 2.0, GV.RR-02 asks for roles, responsibilities and authorities to be established, communicated, understood and enforced. GV.RR-03 expects resources to match the risk strategy, and ID.RA-07 asks for exceptions to be assessed, recorded and tracked. In the EU, NIS2 Article 20 and DORA Article 5 place accountability on the management body rather than on a security team. None of these require a team to go it alone. They require that authority, funding and the exception path are explicit.

Takeaway

A silo is not a team that stopped asking permission. It is a team that stopped asking for help.

Deploying a runtime security tool, an admission controller or an audit pipeline is the easy part, and a platform team can do it independently. Defining what those tools should enforce is a cross-team decision, and pretending otherwise is how the new silo forms.

A simple habit at kick-off: for each row of the baseline, ask who owns the answer, when it is needed and how to reach them. When work stalls, ask what made going alone seem like the best option before assigning blame. Was guidance easy to find? Could the right people respond in time? Was the exception path clear?

Autonomy works best when a team can act, knows where the rest of the answer lives and can reach the people who have it without friction. Trust and collaboration are not the opposite of ownership. They are what make it sustainable.

References

  • Kubernetes, Pod Security Standards and Auditing
  • Falco documentation
  • Kyverno documentation
  • OPA Gatekeeper documentation
  • Sigstore documentation
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSWP 29): GV.RR-02, GV.RR-03, ID.RA-07
  • Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2), Article 20
  • Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA), Article 5

This post describes an engineering operating model, not a legal interpretation or a universal assignment of responsibilities. Adapt it to your organization’s structure and risk management process.

title: 沪深北交易所11月30日下调两融保证金比例至80%

summary: 沪深北交易所将于11月30日正式下调两融保证金比例，从现行的100%降至80%。监管已向券商下发通知，要求做好两融逆周期调节，对保证金比例实施动态管理与差异化控制，及时完成系统参数调整与测试验证，并做好政策解读与风险揭示。
context: 此次下调属于两融逆周期调节安排，券商需确保政策稳妥实施并向投资者充分揭示风险，对A股杠杆资金影响直接。
contentHtml:
沪深北交易所将于11月30日正式下调两融保证金比例，从现行的100%下调至80%。记者最新获悉，监管已向券商下发通知，要求做好两融逆周期调节，包括券商要确保政策稳妥实施，要求各公司基于交易所公布的标准范围，对保证金比例实施动态管理与差异化控制，及时完成系统参数调整与测试验证，并做好政策解读与风险揭示。值得关注的是，通知明确本次保证金比例调整同时适用于新开仓合约及存量合约，投资者不必了结存量合约即可适用新的指标，券商需将相关安排有效传达至投资者，避免因政策理解偏差引发不必要的调仓交易。监管明确，券商要做好客户交易行为管理。通知要求对存在异常交易行为的投资者采取差异化管控，从严适用保证金比例、折算率等风控指标，审慎控制授信规模及交易费率，对频繁异常交易或涉嫌违法违规的投资者依法采取必要限制性措施。

title: Anthropic 承诺投入 9000 亿美元，华尔街预期其债务将为垃圾级
summary: Anthropic 上周募资超 1000 亿美元，估值约 1.18 万亿美元，高于沃尔玛和摩根大通。该公司同时承诺投入 9000 亿美元，但其上市之路颠簸，债券市场前景疑问更大，华尔街预期其债务将为垃圾级。
source: 新浪财经 · 实时滚动
context: AI 头部公司超大规模融资与信用评级担忧并存，凸显资本市场对 AI 行业债务扩张模式的分歧。
contentHtml:
Anthropic的上市之路颠簸。而它在债券市场的前景，疑问更大。

　　这家备受关注的AI企业上周募资超1000亿美元，估值约1.18万亿美元，高于沃尔玛和摩根大通。但它已经承诺，未来数年投入约9000亿美元，为其旗舰AI模型采购海量算力。

　　想要在公司债市场大规模举债并不容易。Anthropic尚未盈利，成立还不到六年，华尔街对它能否履行长期债务义务心存疑虑。债市普遍认为，评级机构会把它的债券定为垃圾级，也就是非投资级。

　　奥斯特韦斯资本管理的债券基金经理克雷格・曼查克表示：“市场对Anthropic任何一笔发债交易都会持审慎态度。一家承诺未来几年要砸9000亿美元的公司，该怎么给它合理定价？”

　　Anthropic的信用评级，会对债券市场乃至整个AI生态产生连锁影响。

　　如果拿到投资级评级，它就可以进入规模8.6万亿美元的高等级公司债市场，这对芯片厂商来说是一大宽慰。博通、英伟达已经为芯片买家提供了数百亿美元的贷款担保，这些芯片最终租给Anthropic、OpenAI这类AI实验室。分析师越来越担心这种循环融资模式以及担保规模，芯片厂商也希望AI实验室可以独立发债融资。

　　AI正在打破一个市场惯例：股权投资者给尚不成熟的科技初创企业出钱，而只拿利息、没有上涨收益的债券投资者会选择回避。数字基建的建设成本极高，有测算称总规模可达10万亿美元，仅靠股市资金已经难以支撑，行业不得不举债。

　　近几周，融资成本上行、信贷收紧，成为重创股市的推手，数万亿美元市值蒸发。Anthropic上周回吐了大部分上市后的涨幅，英伟达、Meta、甲骨文等巨头同样遭遇抛售。

　　一位知名信用投资者担忧，评级机构可能单纯因为它体量巨大就给它投资级评级，使其债券流入本应只持有超低风险资产的养老基金。

　　Anthropic首席执行官达里奥・阿莫代伊周四在接受采访时称：“显然，我们希望未来有一天能够拿到投资级评级。”

　　惠誉、标普全球评级的发言人拒绝置评，Anthropic的发言人同样不予回应。

　　多名大型债券基金经理预计，Anthropic评级大概率落在BB区间，距离投资级还差一到两档。一旦落地，它将成为美国市值最高的高收益债主体。道琼斯市场数据显示，目前这一纪录保持者是希尔顿全球，市值约800亿美元。

　　其他大型AI企业，包括云算力厂商CoreWeave，同样是垃圾级评级，凸显股票投资者和债券投资者对这个行业的巨大分歧。

　　阿波罗全球管理首席执行官马克・罗万在10月接受播客采访时表示：“有些公司市值能到400亿、600亿美元，但发债要付16%至18%的利息。这两者之间，一定有一个估值是错的。”

　　Anthropic这类AI实验室的商业模式还没有完全得到验证，但如果增长持续，它们有可能成长为科技行业的巨头，比肩硅谷老牌企业。2018年，债市同样不看好特斯拉，而之后特斯拉股价迎来大涨。

　　几大评级机构尚未公开表态，最终结果也可能出现分歧，部分机构或许会给出投资级。投资者可能要等到Anthropic首次公开发债之后，才能拿到最终评级结果。

　　基金经理认为，Anthropic不太会大量发行无担保债券，垃圾债市场规模仅1.7万亿美元，而且融资成本很高。

　　PGIM全球信用研究主管布莱恩・巴恩赫斯特称，它更可能继续通过结构化融资、芯片专项融资等方式募资，这类交易可以通过增信手段改善信用条件。

　　但这类融资接下来会变得更难推进，因为市场预期，在前CEO黄仁勋意外离职之后，英伟达会缩减这类担保业务，而黄仁勋正是这类交易的主要推动者。

　　债券基金经理已经难以消化今年大量来自AI大厂、超大规模算力企业的债券，其中不少债券已经出现下跌。SpaceX在6月上市后发行的250亿美元债券，部分品种跌幅已经超过10%。

　　加拿大皇家银行全球资产管理的债券基金经理尼尔・孙说：“我和很多同行交流，大家当下都没有意愿买入这类超大规模算力企业的债券。”

　　Meta、甲骨文这类拥有投资级评级的成熟科技巨头，已经发行创纪录规模的债券，并且为数据中心建设的巨额贷款提供担保。华尔街银行向债基推介时，给出高于普通投资级债券的收益率，但这些资产后续因为市场承接乏力出现贬值。

　　Anthropic或许就是这轮融资热潮的转折点。公司上季度营收170亿美元，但受巨额算力投入拖累依旧亏损，没有其他业务可以给债券投资者提供安全垫。

　　分析师称，公司手头有960亿美元现金，叠加IPO和同步私募的募资款，足以支撑一年以上的支出承诺。它也开始自建算力硬件，这类资产有望帮助它争取投资级评级。SpaceX正是依靠卫星业务拿到了投资级评级。

　　这家AI实验室大约一半的支出承诺，要到2030年才开始兑现。如果到那时还拿不到投资级评级，Anthropic的兑付压力会非常大。

　　尼尔・孙表示：“它还有大约三年时间，争取让投资者认可它的信用逻辑和发展方案，保证资本市场持续对它敞开大门。”

title: 国家发展改革委等部门联合印发《实施全面节约战略行动方案》
summary: 国家发展改革委等部门联合印发《实施全面节约战略行动方案》，以部委联合发文形式部署全面节约战略的实施行动。该文件由国家发改委牵头、多部门联合推出，规格较高。
source: 国家发改委 · 政策通知
context: 多部委联合发文是全面节约战略落地的标志性政策动作，对资源节约与相关行业政策走向具有指引意义。
contentHtml:
国家发展改革委等部门联合印发《实施全面节约战略行动方案》

发布时间：2026/11/04

来源：环资司

[ 打印 ]

　　为深入贯彻党中央和国务院决策部署，推进各类资源节约集约利用，维护国家资源安全，加快经济社会发展全面绿色转型，国家发展改革委、工业和信息化部、自然资源部、水利部、国管局近日联合印发《实施全面节约战略行动方案》（以下简称《方案》）。

　　《方案》坚持以习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想为指导，深入贯彻党的二十大和二十届历次全会精神，完整准确全面贯彻新发展理念，牢固树立节约集约循环利用的资源观，把节约资源贯穿于经济社会发展全过程、各领域，推进资源总量管理、科学配置、全面节约、循环利用，提出了到2030年全面节约工作的主要目标。《方案》突出问题导向，从推进“能水粮地矿材”各类资源要素节约和增强全民节约意识等7个方面，分别提出了重点任务举措。《方案》还明确了标准、政策、监管、科技等支撑保障措施。

　　下一步，国家发展改革委、工业和信息化部、自然资源部、水利部、国管局将会同有关部门加强统筹协调和督促指导，细化目标任务，压实各方责任，扎实推动《方案》各项任务举措落实落地，强化《方案》实施过程中的跟踪评估，充分发挥政府、企业、行业协会、社会公众等各方面作用，形成整体工作合力，不断提高资源利用效率，为全面建设社会主义现代化国家提供坚实资源保障。

title: 国家发改委有关负责同志就《实施全面节约战略行动方案》答记者问
originalTitle: 国家发展改革委有关负责同志就《实施全面节约战略行动方案》答记者问
summary: 国家发展改革委有关负责同志就《实施全面节约战略行动方案》答记者问，对这一全面节约战略的行动方案作出官方解读。该文件由国家发改委层面发布并答疑，是全面节约战略落地实施的重要政策依据。
source: 国家发改委 · 政策通知
context: 全面节约战略属国家顶层部署，发改委官方答疑是把握政策方向与落地节奏的直接依据。
contentHtml:
近日，国家发展改革委、工业和信息化部、自然资源部、水利部、国管局联合印发了《实施全面节约战略行动方案》（以下简称《方案》）。日前，国家发展改革委有关负责同志就《方案》有关情况回答了记者提问。

　　问：《方案》出台的背景是什么？

　　答：节约资源是我国的基本国策。习近平总书记高度重视资源节约工作，多次作出重要指示批示，强调要坚持节约优先，实施全面节约战略，推进各领域节约行动，推动资源利用方式根本转变。近年来，国家发展改革委会同相关部门深入贯彻落实党中央和国务院决策部署，大力实施全面节约战略，推动全面节约工作取得明显成效。“十四五”时期，我国单位国内生产总值能耗、用水量、建设用地使用面积与“十三五”末相比均大幅降低，粮食全产业链各环节损失率明显下降，食品浪费现象得到有效遏制，全社会资源循环利用水平稳步提升。但同时也要看到，资源约束趋紧仍是制约我国经济社会发展的突出问题，资源利用效率有待进一步提高。必须持续深入实施全面节约战略，加强各类资源全过程管理和全链条节约，不断提高资源利用效率。

　　党的二十届三中全会提出，完善资源总量管理和全面节约制度。按照党中央和国务院决策部署，深入实施全面节约战略，推进各类资源节约集约利用，国家发展改革委会同有关部门，在认真做好对标对表、深入开展调查研究、广泛听取意见建议的基础上，起草形成了《方案》，会同工业和信息化部、自然资源部、水利部、国管局等部门联合印发实施。

　　问：《方案》的主要内容是什么？

　　答：《方案》包括9章、22条举措，分为3个部分内容。

　　第一部分是总体要求，为第1章。明确了实施全面节约战略行动的指导思想，提出了到2030年全面节约工作的主要目标。要牢固树立节约集约循环利用的资源观，把节约资源贯穿于经济社会发展全过程、各领域，推进资源总量管理、科学配置、全面节约、循环利用，提高能源、水、粮食、土地、矿产、原材料等资源利用效率。到2030年，我国单位国内生产总值能耗、用水量、建设用地使用面积比2025年分别降低10%左右、10%、15%，粮食全产业链各环节损失率持续降低，主要再生资源年循环利用量达到5.1亿吨，进一步形成崇尚节约的社会风尚。

　　第二部分是重点任务，包括第2章至第8章。聚焦重点问题，从推进“能水粮地矿材”各类资源要素节约和增强全民节约意识等7个方面，分别提出了重点任务举措。一是深入推进能源节约和能效提升。遏制能源消费总量不合理增长，大力推进重点领域节能。二是强化水资源节约高效利用。全面落实水资源刚性约束制度，推进重点领域深度节水。三是深化粮食节约和反食品浪费。强化生产储存环节节约减损，降低运输加工环节损失，坚决遏制餐饮消费浪费。四是推进土地资源节约集约利用。严格国土空间用途管制，提高集约高效利用水平，盘活利用存量土地。五是提升矿产资源开发利用水平。推进绿色勘查开采，加强矿产资源综合利用。六是加强原材料节约和回收循环利用。推进绿色设计和绿色制造，加快提升资源化利用水平，持续扩大再利用规模。七是培育崇尚节约社会风尚。加强公共机构示范引领，推广绿色生活方式，深化宣传教育引导。

　　第三部分是支撑保障，为第9章。明确了标准、政策、监管、科技等支撑保障措施，包括完善法律和标准体系、加大政策支持力度、加强监督管理执法、强化科技创新支撑等。

　　问：《方案》有哪些特点？

　　答：《方案》坚持目标导向和问题导向，把握新形势下保障资源安全要求，树立“能水粮地矿材”一体化节约理念，推进全过程管理和全链条节约，构建有利于节约资源的空间布局、产业结构、生产方式、生活方式。

　　一是完善制度政策体系，推动制度约束更为刚性。《方案》针对当前节约相关制度政策体系不完善的问题，明确推动修订节约能源法、循环经济促进法、公共机构节能条例等法律法规，以及严格执行固定资产投资项目节能审查和碳排放评价办法、建立健全涉及水资源开发利用的有关规划水资源论证制度、健全国土空间规划动态评估调整机制等分领域规章制度，为实施全面节约战略提供有力制度保障。

　　二是提高资源利用效率，推动资源安全更有保障。《方案》聚焦“能水粮地矿材”各类资源要素节约面临的利用方式粗放、利用效率不高等突出问题，明确了15项重点任务举措，推动“十五五”时期我国单位国内生产总值能耗、用水量、建设用地使用面积进一步降低，粮食全产业链各环节损失率持续降低，资源利用效率稳步提高。

　　三是增强全民节约意识，推动绿色生活更加普及。《方案》针对当前生活中浪费现象仍然突出等问题，提出坚持公共机构带头、公众参与、社会共治，推广绿色生活方式，深化宣传教育引导，营造厉行节约、反对浪费浓厚氛围，进一步形成崇尚节约的社会风尚。

　　问：下一步如何推动《方案》实施？

　　答：资源节约工作涉及面广、环节多、链条长，是一项复杂的系统工程，需多部门协同推进、地方政府抓好落实、社会公众广泛参与。

　　下一步，国家发展改革委将会同工业和信息化部、自然资源部、水利部、国管局等部门加强统筹协调，强化督促指导，细化目标任务，压实各方责任，扎实推动《方案》各项任务举措落实落地，强化《方案》实施过程中的跟踪评估，充分发挥政府、企业、行业协会、社会公众等各方面作用，形成整体工作合力，不断提高资源利用效率，为全面建设社会主义现代化国家提供坚实资源保障。

title: 你的 OpenTelemetry 管道正在变成性能瓶颈吗？
originalTitle: Is your OpenTelemetry pipeline becoming a performance bottleneck?
summary: 作者在 CNCF Blog 分享其在 Cloud Native Days Austria 2026 上的演讲《How to Defeat OTel's Silent Killer: The Performance Overhead》，聚焦 OpenTelemetry 管道的性能开销问题。演讲指出，构建可观测性管道时数据采集（collecting）的开销是一个容易被忽视的问题。
context: 性能开销被称为 OTel 的“隐形杀手”，对大规模运行可观测性管道的工程团队具有直接参考价值。
contentHtml:
Posted on November 17, 2026 by Diana Todea (CNCF Ambassador, OpenTelemetry Documentation approver, Romanian Localization maintainer)

At Cloud Native Days Austria 2026, I presented a talk called How to Defeat OTel’s Silent Killer: The Performance Overhead, exploring a problem that is easy to overlook when building observability pipelines: the cost of collecting telemetry itself.

OpenTelemetry has become a cornerstone of cloud-native observability, providing standardized APIs, SDKs, and tooling for generating, collecting, processing, and exporting metrics, logs, and traces. However, instrumentation and telemetry processing are not free. Every span created, attribute attached, and batch exported consumes resources.

As applications scale, poorly configured telemetry pipelines can introduce significant CPU usage, memory pressure, network traffic, and storage costs. In some cases, the infrastructure responsible for observing a system can become a performance problem of its own.

The good news is that much of this overhead can be understood, measured, and reduced without sacrificing the visibility engineers depend on.

Where does OpenTelemetry overhead come from?

When discussing OpenTelemetry performance, we often focus on the application SDK. However, the cost extends beyond instrumentation.

The entire telemetry pipeline contributes to resource consumption, from generating spans and collecting metrics to processing, exporting, and storing data.

Instrumentation overhead is also workload-dependent. Two applications using the same instrumentation libraries can experience very different results depending on request throughput, attribute volume, runtime behavior, and the number of spans generated per request.

This is why relying on a single overhead percentage can be misleading. Instead, we should examine CPU consumption, memory usage, application latency, telemetry volume, and the behavior of the Collector under load.

There is also an important trade-off between application safety and telemetry completeness. When a pipeline becomes overloaded, backpressure and memory safeguards can protect the application and OpenTelemetry Collector, but they may also lead to rejected or dropped telemetry.

The objective is not simply to minimize resource consumption. It is to maintain useful observability while keeping its operational cost predictable.

Investigating the Collector: five common configuration problems

For my demonstration, I used Telemetrygen, an OpenTelemetry utility that generates synthetic telemetry, to investigate how Collector configuration affects resource consumption.

The investigation focused on five common sources of unnecessary overhead.

1. Inefficient batching

Exporting small amounts of telemetry frequently can increase serialization work, export requests, and network overhead.

The OpenTelemetry Collector groups telemetry inside the exporter’s sending queue before transmitting it downstream, helping amortize this work across larger payloads. (Note: Historically, this was handled by a standalone batch processor, which is now deprecated in favor of built-in exporter batching).

However, batching parameters should reflect the actual workload. Larger batches are not automatically better: they can increase buffering requirements and affect export latency.

exporters:
  otlp_grpc:
    endpoint: "otel-backend:4317"
    sending_queue:
      enabled: true
      sizer: items       
      queue_size: 100000 
      batch:
        enabled: true
        min_size: 8192
        flush_timeout: 200ms

Configuring batch inside an exporter’s sending_queue groups spans, metrics, or logs before forwarding them downstream, improving compression efficiency and durability while reducing export overhead. Batches are sent when a configured size threshold is reached or a timeout expires.

In this example, min_size: 8192 triggers an export when the batch reaches 8,192 items, while flush_timeout: 200ms triggers an export regardless of batch size. Once batching is enabled, these values are the Collector’s documented defaults, not universal performance recommendations. (Note: Because unbatched requests enter the queue first in this architecture, this example switches sizer from the default requests to items with a queue_size of 100000 to prevent smaller, unbatched bursts from overflowing the queue).

The important point is to measure how batching affects resource consumption and throughput rather than relying on example configurations.

2. Unnecessary resource attributes

Resource attributes provide valuable context about the systems producing telemetry. But collecting and forwarding attributes that nobody uses can increase payload sizes and downstream processing costs.

For example, an application might need host.name, host.arch, and os.type for troubleshooting, but not detailed hardware information such as host.cpu.model.name or host.cpu.cache.l2.size.

The OpenTelemetry Collector’s resource detection processor allows engineers to configure which system attributes are collected. Disabling unnecessary attributes can reduce telemetry volume and processing overhead, although the impact on storage and cardinality depends on the backend.

A practical example: Keep the hostname and operating system type, but disable CPU model and cache metadata when those details are not needed for troubleshooting.

3. Aggressive receiver polling

Infrastructure receivers collect metrics at configured intervals, often independently of application traffic.

Polling host metrics, container statistics, databases, and network services every few seconds creates continuous work even when applications are relatively idle.

Increasing collection intervals from 10 to 30 seconds, where operational requirements permit, can reduce collection frequency and associated overhead.

This introduces a trade-off: lower polling frequency means less temporal resolution. The appropriate interval depends on how quickly a metric changes and how it is used for troubleshooting or alerting.

4. Exporting every trace

Not every successful request needs to produce a trace that is retained.

Exporting all traces can consume significant bandwidth, Collector resources, and backend capacity, particularly in high-throughput applications.

Sampling provides a way to control this volume.

Head-based sampling makes decisions early, reducing downstream work. Tail-based sampling makes decisions after observing more of a trace, enabling policies that retain errors or other diagnostically interesting requests.

These policies retain traces with an error status and probabilistically sample 5% of traces, including potentially some additional error traces. However, tail sampling is not free. It requires buffering trace data until a decision can be made, introducing additional memory and processing overhead. 

Choosing a sampling strategy means balancing cost, diagnostic value, and the resources needed to make sampling decisions.

5. Memory safeguards applied too late

The OpenTelemetry Collector includes a memory_limiter processor to help manage memory pressure.

Processor ordering matters. When enrichment and transformation processors run before memory limiting, the Collector may perform additional work on telemetry that is subsequently refused under memory pressure.

Memory limiting is a protective mechanism rather than a performance optimization in itself. Its purpose is to improve stability under pressure, not necessarily to reduce CPU consumption during normal operation. Placing the memory limiter early in the pipeline helps apply safeguards before more expensive processing. 

It is important to understand that the memory limiter is not a substitute for appropriate resource limits or capacity planning. It can refuse incoming data when memory pressure becomes excessive, and receivers must handle this behavior correctly to avoid unnecessary telemetry loss.

From local experiments to production architecture

Optimizing a single Collector is only part of the solution.

In Kubernetes, telemetry workloads can fluctuate significantly as applications scale, deployments change, and traffic increases. A Collector configuration that performs well under synthetic load may behave differently in production.

Here are some architectural practices that can help address these challenges.

  1. Separate collection from centralized processing. A two-tier architecture can use lightweight edge Collectors for local collection and gateway Collectors for more expensive processing. This allows different parts of the pipeline to scale according to their workloads.
  2. Control telemetry volume early. Filtering unnecessary attributes, removing unneeded data, and avoiding excessive cardinality can reduce the amount of information processed and transferred downstream. These decisions should preserve the context required for debugging and correlation.
  3. Plan for memory pressure and backend outages. Kubernetes memory limits, Collector memory safeguards, bounded queues, and retry mechanisms serve different purposes. Persistent queues can improve resilience during temporary backend failures, but they still require capacity planning and cannot guarantee delivery under every failure scenario.
  4. Scale with signal-specific requirements in mind. Horizontal scaling can increase throughput, but stateful processing requires additional consideration. Tail sampling, for example, generally requires spans belonging to the same trace to reach the same processing instance.

These architectural decisions are just as important as tuning individual processors.

Don’t forget the instrumentation

One of the most effective optimizations happens before telemetry reaches the Collector.

Instrumentation should answer meaningful operational questions rather than collect everything simply because it is possible. Excessive spans, high-cardinality attributes, and unnecessary instrumentation can increase resource consumption throughout the entire pipeline.

For metrics, attributes containing unbounded values such as unique request IDs can create large numbers of distinct time series. For traces and logs, excessive attributes and events increase payload sizes and may affect backend processing or indexing costs.

Why I chose Telemetrygen for my demo

When preparing my performance investigation, I initially considered using the official OpenTelemetry Astronomy Shop. While it is an excellent environment for exploring instrumentation across microservices, its multiple applications, databases, and supporting services introduce additional CPU and memory consumption.

For this experiment, I wanted to isolate the Collector’s performance overhead without the background noise of a complete application environment.

Instead, I chose Telemetrygen, a lightweight utility for generating synthetic traces, metrics, and logs at controlled rates.

In my OpenTelemetry performance overhead demo, I used synthetic telemetry to investigate how Collector configuration affects resource consumption. The demonstration walks through common inefficiencies, including missing batching, unnecessary resource attributes, aggressive receiver polling, excessive trace export, and memory limiter placement, showing how targeted configuration changes can improve pipeline efficiency.

This approach helped isolate Collector behavior, but it is only one part of the performance picture. For understanding instrumentation overhead inside real applications, a complete environment such as Astronomy Shop remains valuable.

Exploring instrumentation further

Reducing overhead starts with understanding what telemetry an application generates and why. The official OpenTelemetry instrumentation documentation introduces automatic and manual instrumentation, while the sampling documentation explains how to control trace volume. These are useful starting points for reviewing instrumentation decisions before optimizing the Collector itself.

For engineers interested in investigating performance further, the OpenTelemetry Collector documentation covers pipeline configuration and processing. The OpenTelemetry community is also a good place to discuss performance challenges. The Collector SIG focuses on Collector architecture, performance, and configuration, with discussions taking place in the #otel-collector channel on CNCF Slack.

For questions about instrumentation overhead in a specific programming language, the corresponding language SIG is a better starting point. The OpenTelemetry community page provides information about SIGs, public meetings, and how to get involved.

Making performance part of observability design

OpenTelemetry overhead is not a single problem with a single configuration fix.

It is the combined effect of instrumentation decisions, data volume, processor configuration, export behavior, and infrastructure architecture.

The most useful lesson from this investigation is that observability pipelines should be measured and optimized like any other production system.

Start with controlled benchmarks. Understand where resources are consumed. Introduce configuration changes individually, and evaluate their impact on CPU, memory, latency, throughput, and telemetry loss.

Most importantly, treat example configurations as starting points rather than production-ready defaults.

OpenTelemetry gives us the tools to understand complex distributed systems. With thoughtful instrumentation, careful pipeline configuration, and appropriate scaling strategies, we can ensure that collecting this information does not become an unnecessary burden on the systems we are trying to observe.

title: Kyverno 的 CEL 准入成本究竟花在哪：Kubernetes 准入控制优化剖析
originalTitle: Optimizing Kubernetes admission control: Where Kyverno’s CEL admission cost actually goes
summary: Kyverno 团队对 Kubernetes 准入路径进行性能剖析，发现约 86% 的成本并不在 CEL 策略表达式求值环节，与其为求值而设计的预期相反。文章据此拆解 Kyverno CEL 准入开销的真实去向，为准入控制优化提供依据。
context: Kyverno 是 CNCF 生态主流的 Kubernetes 策略引擎，这项官方剖析对大规模集群的策略性能调优有直接参考价值。
contentHtml:
CNCF projects highlighted in this post

Kyverno’s CEL (Common Expression Language)-based engines exist to evaluate policy expressions. So when we profiled the admission path, we expected to find the bulk of the cost in CEL evaluation.

It was not there. About 86% of what the engine allocated went into preparing the object for evaluation, and almost none of it into evaluating policy.

We went looking because a public benchmark put Kyverno behind the alternatives. Those benchmarks measured the legacy ClusterPolicy JMESPath engine, which did have a real regression at the time, and the usual answer was to point people at the newer CEL-based engine instead. That answer was right but incomplete: we had not checked what the CEL engine itself was spending its time on.

This post is about where that performance cost came from, why it grew with the number of policies you deploy, and what removing it did. The fix ships in Kyverno 1.19.2.

Please read the limitations section before you quote any number here. And as always, run your own tests in your environments, for real-world accuracy.

What the profile showed

Kyverno’s CEL engines evaluate policies against a CEL activation: a set of variables your policy expressions can reference. One of those variables is request, the AdmissionRequest the API server sent, converted into the unstructured map form CEL understands.

Here is a heap profile of the ValidatingPolicy engine handling admission requests, before and after the change, by share of total allocated bytes:

Before, ConvertObjectToUnstructured accounted for 86.8% of everything the engine allocated. CEL evaluation itself barely registered. After, object conversion falls to 2.9%, and the largest single frame becomes evaluateWithData — the code that actually runs your policy expressions.

The same pattern shows up in the MutatingPolicy engine, which was paying a smaller but still substantial version of the same cost:

One caveat on reading those profiles: the post-fix benchmark completes more iterations in the same time because it is faster, so the two profiles have different absolute totals. Compare the shares, not the raw bytes. Per-request figures come from the benchmark table further down.

Why: the same object, converted once per policy

The API server sends the admitted object as raw JSON bytes. CEL cannot read bytes, so Kyverno parses them into the map form CEL understands before it can evaluate anything against them.

That conversion happened inside the loop over matched policies rather than before it. With the Pod Security Standards set, roughly 16 policies match a typical Pod creation — so Kyverno parsed the same Pod 16 times, same input, same output, every time. The cost grew with your policy count and with the size of the object being admitted: O(policies), where it should have been O(1).

The object does not change between policies. There was never a reason to convert it more than once.

The fix: convert once per request

The change moves the conversion out of the per-policy loop. Kyverno builds the CEL request value once, before the loop starts, and every matched policy reuses it.

Doing that without changing what policies see takes some care. The expensive part of the conversion is the admitted object itself, so Kyverno converts a copy of the request with that object temporarily blanked out — which leaves only cheap fields to walk — and splices the object back in afterwards. The same conversion code still produces the result, so the output matches what policies saw before rather than being a reimplementation that someone has to keep in sync by hand.

Keeping policy behavior identical

The first attempt used a single shared builder for every CEL engine. Testing caught that this quietly changed how policies behave, because the engines had never agreed on what request.object meant in the first place.

Validating and generating policies saw the object exactly as the API server sent it. Mutating policies saw a normalized version. The two also disagreed about what an empty object looks like to CEL, which matters for operations like DELETE where one side is absent.

Unifying them would have changed the result of expressions people already have deployed. That is a conversation worth having, but not one a performance fix should start on its own. So each engine keeps the contract it already had, sharing one fast implementation underneath.

Equivalence tests pin this down: they run the original code as the reference and compare its output against the new one field by field, across every request type, so any drift fails the build.

What changed

The benchmark calls the engine directly with a roughly 50 KB Pod and a varying number of matched policies. It times the engine alone — building the request value, matching, and evaluating CEL. It does not include the webhook round trip, the API server, or etcd, so these are not end-to-end admission latencies.

The MutatingPolicy engine improves on the same curve, from 258,943 to 52,689 allocations and 10.59 ms to 2.97 ms at 64 policies.

The slope is the point, not the headline multiple. Before the change, allocations grew about 63 times going from 1 policy to 64. After, about 10 times — and that residual growth is CEL evaluation, which is the work you deployed the policies to get. Object preparation is now constant per request instead of proportional to how many policies you run.

Practically: adding policies to a Kyverno deployment used to carry a hidden per-policy serialization cost on top of the evaluation you asked for. It no longer does.

Image verification too

The image verification engine had the same pattern, with its own private copy of the conversion code, so it got the same fix. The gain there is memory rather than speed: image verification spends most of its time fetching signatures and attestations over the network, and that part does not change.

How this compares to native admission policies

With the per-policy tax gone, it is worth asking where Kyverno’s CEL engine actually sits against the API server’s own ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.

Running the same 16 Pod Security Standards policies through both engines on one cluster, the answer depends on how many policies you enforce:

At one policy, native is ahead: about 9.2 ms against Kyverno’s 12.8 ms. At the full 16-policy set, Kyverno is ahead: about 20 ms against native’s 29 ms.

Those numbers were measured on Kyverno 1.19.0, which predates the change described above. The Kyverno side of that chart should now be better than shown; we have not re-run the comparison.

The two engines pay their costs differently. Native dispatches each policy separately on the API server, so its cost grows with the number of policies you enforce. Kyverno pays once per request to receive the object over a webhook, and that cost is shared across however many policies then evaluate. With only a policy or two, native is ahead. Once you are running a realistic set, Kyverno matches it and can come out ahead.

That framing only became accurate with this fix. Kyverno’s cost was not fixed per request before it — it was per policy, which is exactly why the curve looked the way it did.

The CPU side is more one-sided. Under matched load, Kyverno’s engine used about 3.2 cores against the API server’s 8.2 for native. The surprise in the API server profile is that 67% of its CPU sits in the policy dispatch machinery while the actual CEL bytecode execution is about 5.5% — the cost is dispatching 16 policies and building an input for each, not evaluating them. And that load lands on the control plane, which you cannot scale horizontally the way you can scale a Kyverno deployment.

Both numbers come from a single-host setup where the webhook hop is loopback and effectively free. On a real multi-node cluster that hop costs real latency on every Kyverno request, which narrows the latency gap and matters most at low policy counts. The CPU finding does not depend on topology.

The legacy engine, briefly

The benchmarks that prompted this work measured ClusterPolicy, the older non-CEL engine, so it is worth saying what happened there.

We reproduced the regression across four releases, each on a fresh cluster, run in shuffled order over eight rounds so no version was systematically favored, and compared everything against 1.13.6.

The regression is real — between 12% and 23% depending on load — and it appears between 1.16.4 and 1.17.0. That is where the engine started copying its entire evaluation context on every checkpoint, in order to fix a separate bug where one rule’s data could leak into the next.

The fix keeps that guarantee but stops paying for it upfront: it takes a shallow snapshot and only copies a value when something actually writes to it. The benchmark returns to roughly its pre-regression level, and the rule isolation still holds, pinned by a test that fails on the old code.

This ships in 1.19.2 alongside the CEL work, and only there. The legacy engine is on its way out, so the effort belongs in the engine replacing it.

What this does not fix

  • The engine still pays one JSON round-trip of the admitted object per request, to preserve the raw, un-normalized parse that request.object has always exposed. Evaluating against the typed object, or a cheaper representation, would remove even that — but it would change what policies see, so it needs its own design.
  • Mutating policies thread full objects between policies rather than propagating a patch diff. A patch-only model is a substantially larger redesign and is not implemented.
  • Tail latency under sustained load on a single replica is not addressed by any of this, and we have not re-measured it since. If you have seen Kyverno’s p95 swing widely between runs at high load, that is a separate problem and it is still open.

Limitations

  • Single machine. Everything here reproduces the relationship between configurations, not the absolute numbers you would see on a 32-core server.
  • Most of this is a Go benchmark. The allocation and timing figures come from benchmarks driving the real engine loop, and the profiles come from those benchmark runs. They isolate the engine cleanly, and they exclude network, serialization at the webhook boundary, and etcd.
  • The engine comparison uses loopback, so the webhook network hop is excluded, and dry-run, so the etcd write is excluded.
  • The native side runs Kyverno’s generated policies, which is a faithful same-policy comparison rather than a hand-tuned native policy set.
  • Side controllers were disabled in these runs. Only the admission controller was active.

Reproduce it

The harness is in the Kyverno repository under docs/perf-testing/: the version ladder, the pinned Pod Security Standards policy set, the k6 scripts, and the cluster setup. The engine benchmarks live beside the code they measure, in pkg/cel/policies/vpol/engine and pkg/engine/context.

If you benchmark Kyverno and get a result you do not like, please publish it — with the method, the caveats, and the per-trial numbers.

Conclusion

Our mission at Kyverno is to be the best policy engine for Kubernetes and beyond. Admission control is a critical process in Kubernetes clusters, and a slow or misconfigured controller can impact cluster operations. Thanks to our community, we have fixed performance issues and added more tests. For future releases, we will be looking at improving concurrency and further optimization.

Thanks to Mustafa Erdinç, whose comparison of different Kubernetes policy engines motivated this work.

References

  • #17572 — build the request activation once per admission request
  • #17585 — hoist the request-map build in the image verification engine
  • #17565 — reduce engine context checkpoint copy cost

title: 如何在不受你控制的 Kubernetes 环境中支持你的应用
originalTitle: How to support your app on Kubernetes environments you don’t control
summary: CNCF 博客文章讲解如何为客户运行、不受你掌控的 Kubernetes 环境中的应用提供支持，并指出这与自己集群里运行应用是两回事。文章点出核心难点在于你无法控制集群配置、升级节奏和周边工具。
context: 面向需要为多客户集群交付和支持软件的团队，切中供应商难以掌控运行环境的常见痛点。
contentHtml:
CNCF projects highlighted in this post

Running an application in Kubernetes is one thing, but supporting that application in Kubernetes environments your customers run is something else entirely. You don’t control the cluster configuration, its upgrade schedule, the surrounding tooling, or the process for investigating an incident. But customers will still look to you when your application won’t install, an upgrade breaks, or a workload behaves differently in their environment than they expected.

That doesn’t mean customer-managed Kubernetes deployments can’t work, but it does mean support has to account for the variation you’ll see in real clusters.

No Two Customer Environments Are Alike

You’ll definitely have two customers (or more!) who both say they run Kubernetes and yet have very different environments.

One may run a managed Kubernetes service in a public cloud. Another may operate its own infrastructure. They may use different Kubernetes versions, networking configurations, ingress controllers, storage classes, image registries, security policies, observability tools, or access controls.

Those differences affect how your application deploys and how your team supports it. A chart that installs cleanly in your reference architecture may fail because a customer’s admission policies reject a required permission, their storage configuration doesn’t meet your application’s requirements, or their cluster runs a Kubernetes version you haven’t tested yet or no longer support.

Unfortunately, your customer still experiences that as a problem with your application. That’s why your team needs a documented view of what the application requires from the cluster, and what falls outside the support boundary.

At a minimum, customers need to know:

  • Which Kubernetes versions and distributions you support
  • Which permissions, policies, and cluster capabilities the application needs
  • What networking, ingress, DNS, certificate, secret management, and storage configuration the application expects
  • What resources the application needs to run reliably
  • Which logs, events, metrics, and configuration details your support team will need during an escalation. With bonus points for providing commands directly.

The goal isn’t to make every customer environment identical (you can’t). Instead, you need to define a supported operating model so every deployment doesn’t turn into a new discovery process for your customer support team.

Customers Won’t Upgrade on Your Schedule

Your application roadmap may assume customers will move to newer Kubernetes versions quickly. A quick reality check: most won’t.

Customers have their own release schedules, validation processes, maintenance windows, compliance requirements, internal dependencies, and risk thresholds. Even when they want to upgrade, their platform team may have a long list of cluster add-ons, integrations, and workloads to validate first.

Like any other software, Kubernetes and different components in its ecosystem change over time. APIs are deprecated and removed, version compatibility varies across control-plane and node components, and the upstream project supports release branches for only the three most recent minor releases.

Your team needs a compatibility policy that answers a few basic questions:

  • Which Kubernetes versions do you support today?
  • Which versions are approaching the end of support?
  • How much notice do customers get before you stop supporting a version?
  • What does a customer need to do if an application release depends on a newer Kubernetes capability?
  • Can you offer a documented workaround when a customer can’t upgrade immediately?

If the answer to every compatibility problem is to update Kubernetes, customers will quickly find that your support isn’t aligned with how they operate. Your team needs to explain what’s incompatible, why it matters, and the easiest path to return to a supported configuration.

Kubernetes Expertise Has to Be Customer-Facing

A general application support team can’t diagnose every Kubernetes issue. When a product runs inside a cluster your customer manages, customer-facing teams need enough Kubernetes depth to identify where the problem really lives.

That doesn’t mean every support employee has to operate production clusters. It does mean someone working directly with customers needs to understand the difference between an application issue, a deployment-configuration issue, and a cluster-level issue.

For example, a pod stuck in Pending may point to unavailable capacity, resource requests that don’t fit on available nodes, a scheduling constraint, or a policy that prevents placement. An image pull failure may involve registry access, credentials, network connectivity, or image policy enforcement. Those details determine who needs to take the next action and what evidence they need to act on it.

Your customer-facing team needs dedicated Kubernetes expertise that can:

  • Ask for the right diagnostic information early
  • Review Kubernetes events, pod status, and relevant logs
  • Identify when a customer platform, security, networking, or infrastructure team needs to get involved
  • Explain the issue in terms each stakeholder can act on
  • Escalate to engineering with enough environmental context to investigate effectively

Getting accurate answers to these questions matters because the person opening a support case may not own the cluster. The application team probably owns the deployment. A platform team probably owns Kubernetes. Security owns policies. Another infrastructure team may own networking, storage, or identity. Someone on your team needs to help move the issue between those groups.

Build for Variation

You can’t control every Kubernetes environment where customers run your application. You can control whether your support model treats that variation as expected or as a surprise.

So make sure you have a plan for it by:

  1. Defining what you support.
  2. Documenting the requirements that matter.
  3. Testing the Kubernetes versions and deployment conditions you commit to supporting.
  4. Setting a clear upgrade and deprecation policy.
  5. Making Kubernetes expertise available during onboarding, deployment, escalation, and ongoing support.

The support model changes when a provider manages the Kubernetes layer alongside the customer. Instead of troubleshooting an application across an unknown mix of cluster configurations, versions, networking, and add-ons, the provider and customer can work from a more clearly defined operating foundation.

title: 当同步窗口关闭时：Argo CD self-heal 如何跳过了迁移钩子
originalTitle: When a sync window closes: How Argo CD self-heal skipped the migration hook
summary: CNCF 博客复盘了一个真实案例：客户在同步窗口关闭期间推送版本，Argo CD 报告 sync 成功，但迁移钩子实际没有执行。文章逐步拆解了 self-heal 机制跳过该迁移钩子的具体过程与原因。
context: sync 窗口与 hook 的交互是 Argo CD GitOps 实践中的隐蔽坑点，对平台和运维团队很有参考价值。
contentHtml:
CNCF projects highlighted in this post

The uncomfortable question

A few days ago, a customer asked me a question that sounded simple: “Argo CD said the sync succeeded, so why didn’t our migration run?” They had pushed a release while a deny sync window was active. When the window opened, five regional Applications rolled out the same commit. Three of them ran the database migration. Two did not, and the new code spent the next 36 to 44 minutes talking to a schema it did not understand.

My first instinct was to blame something specific to their setup. I was wrong. It took me two days, a throwaway lab, and a careful read of the Argo CD source to see that this is not bad luck. It is a race, and with the right timing, anyone can lose it.

Synced, healthy, and wrong

What bothered me most was how normal everything looked. The two broken Applications were Synced and Healthy on the new commit. Their last operation said “successfully synced (all tasks run)”. If you only looked at the UI, you would have signed off on the release.

The setup itself was ordinary. One service, five regions, one Application per region, automated sync with prune and self-heal turned on. Production sat behind a deny window outside business hours, and the migration ran as a Sync hook Job, which is exactly how many of us were taught to do it.

The only clue was buried in the controller log. The two bad operations listed thirteen specific resources and carried a self-heal attempt count of one. In other words, Argo CD had not deployed a release. It had healed drift, and healing drift never runs hooks.

A lab you can break on purpose

I don’t trust an explanation until I can make the failure happen on demand, so I built the smallest setup I could.

The app was as plain as I could make it. One Application with automated sync, prune, and self-heal. A ConfigMap and a Deployment that carry a release string, so every release makes the app OutOfSync. And a migration that runs as a Sync hook, labelled with its release so I could see at a glance which one last ran:

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migration
  labels:
    release: "v11"
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: Sync
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: BeforeHookCreation
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo migrating schema to v11; sleep 3"]

The last piece was a deny window on the project, four minutes long and starting at the current minute, so I knew to the second when it would close.

My first attempt did not reproduce anything, and that turned out to be the most useful run of the day. The app’s periodic refresh landed in the same second as my trigger, won the race, and did a perfectly correct full sync. So I changed the script. I pushed release v11 while the window was active, and refreshed the app fifteen seconds before the close to push its next periodic refresh a couple of minutes out.

The app synced v11 in one second, and the UI looked spotless.

Then I opened the migration Job. It still said release: v10.

I reproduced it five times out of six. The failure was not rare. It only needed the wrong event to arrive first.

The first refresh wins

With debug logging on, the story was right there. Argo CD refreshes an Application for two very different reasons. A level-2 refresh comes from the reconciliation timer, roughly every two to three minutes, and compares the app against Git. A level-1 refresh comes from a change to a managed object and reuses what the controller already knows. When a window closes, nothing announces it. The next refresh of either kind simply finds that syncing is allowed again, and whichever kind arrives first decides what happens next.

During the window, the timer-driven refreshes keep comparing the new commit and record it in status.sync.revision, while the last real sync stays on the old commit. A level-1 refresh then uses that same recorded revision as the one to compare, checks it against itself in evaluateRevisionChanges, and concludes there are no changes. With no changes, alreadyAttemptedSync only compares the Application’s source, which has not changed either, so the controller decides it already synced this revision. With self-heal on, that means healing drift: a sync of only the out-of-sync resources, which is a partial sync, which skips hooks and writes no history.

A timer-driven refresh compares against targetRevision instead, notices that the last synced revision is older, and runs a normal full sync with hooks. The bug fits in one sentence. On the level-1 path, the last compared revision is mistaken for the last synced one.

A hook is not a guarantee

It is tempting to reach for a quick fix inside the hook model. Make the migration a PreSync hook instead of a Sync hook. Turn on the newer RunHooksOnPartialSync option. Shorten the window. From what I read in the code, none of these change the outcome. A partial sync skips every hook type, the new option is ignored for automated syncs, and self-heal is automated by definition. The race happens at every window close, whatever its length. I didn’t test these three, but the code leaves little room for doubt.

The real lesson is broader than this bug. A hook runs when a particular kind of operation runs. If the release can reach the cluster through any other kind of operation, the hook is a hope, not a guarantee.

Make the migration part of the desired state

The fix I now recommend is to stop treating the migration as a side effect of syncing and make it part of what gets synced. Remove the hook annotations, give the Job a sync wave that runs before the app, and give it a name that changes every release.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migration-v11            # change per release
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"

Now the migration is an ordinary managed resource. A new release brings a Job that does not exist yet, so any sync, partial or full, sees it as missing and applies it, and Argo CD waits for that wave to be healthy before it touches the next one. In my lab, the wave version went through the exact broken self-heal path, and the migration still finished, one second before the new ConfigMap and Deployment were applied. The previous release’s Job was pruned on the way.

There are a few details worth getting right. Use a unique name per release, such as the image tag in a Helm template, because a Job’s pod template is immutable. Keep prune on so old Jobs are cleaned up. Don’t set ttlSecondsAfterFinished, or Kubernetes will delete the Job, self-heal will see a missing resource, and your migration will run again. Keep migrations idempotent anyway. And try a deliberately failing migration in staging before you rely on this, because that is the one case I did not test.

Or let the timer decide

If changing every chart is not an option this week, there is a blunter tool. Turn off self-heal on the apps that run migrations.

syncPolicy:
  automated:
    prune: true
    selfHeal: false

I ran two apps through the same window to compare. Both made the same faulty “no changes” decision. The one with self-heal on deployed v11 without its migration. The one with self-heal off logged “Skipping auto-sync: most recent sync already to […]” and simply waited. About two minutes later, its timer-driven refresh compared against the real last sync and ran a full sync with the hook, and the v11 migration finished.

No manual sync, and no window of mismatched code and schema, because the app stayed entirely on the old release while it waited. The price is drift correction. Anyone who edits a resource by hand now leaves it OutOfSync until the next commit.

Trust the sync, not the timing

Sync windows, self-heal, and hooks are each reasonable on their own. Together they leave a gap that opens at every window close, and whether you fall into it depends on which event reaches the controller first. I don’t think you should have to win a race to get a correct release.

So I stopped letting a hook be the only thing that runs a migration. If the schema change is part of the desired state, every path that syncs the release also syncs the migration. We do not need to trust the timing. We need to trust what we put in Git.

References

  • Argo CD docs: Sync Windows
  • Argo CD docs: Resource Hooks
  • Argo CD docs: Sync Phases and Waves

title: OpenShell 加入 CNCF：以开放治理保障 Agentic AI 安全
originalTitle: Welcoming OpenShell to the CNCF: Open Governance to Secure Agentic AI
summary: 在 KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 上，CNCF 接纳 NVIDIA 捐赠的 OpenShell 为 Sandbox 项目。OpenShell 是一个用于保护和治理自主 AI 代理的开源运行时，项目将以开放治理模式推进 Agentic AI 的安全化。
context: 头部芯片厂商将智能体 AI 安全治理开源并捐赠给云原生基金会，显示 Agentic AI 安全正成为云原生社区的新议题。
contentHtml:
CNCF projects highlighted in this post

Today at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) welcomes OpenShell as a Sandbox project. NVIDIA has contributed OpenShell, an open source runtime for securing and governing autonomous AI agents, to the foundation’s community-led home.

As organizations put AI agents to work, they need to give agents real capability without giving them unchecked access to data, secrets, or networks. This requires enforcement outside of the agents, right within the infrastructure that the agents run on. 

OpenShell does exactly that: it manages and monitors agent behavior, provides and enforces policy-based boundaries for what it can do. OpenShell is adopting Cedar, another CNCF project, as its policy language. It’s a great example of CNCF projects building on one another.

Why this belongs in the cloud native community

Agents are becoming part of cloud native infrastructure, and the layer that governs them should be shared, vendor-neutral, and open to everyone who depends on it. OpenShell already reflects that spirit. Core contributors from NVIDIA, Red Hat, Docker, and Canonical have worked on the project since its inception. Their early involvement, alongside many additional organizations adopting OpenShell shows broad industry agreement on the need for dependable controls for agentic systems.

“Open source is the foundation of enterprise trust. As agents become part of cloud native infrastructure, the controls around them need to be open, auditable, and built together with the ecosystem. Bringing OpenShell to the CNCF puts governance of the project in the hands of the community. Red Hat has always believed that innovation thrives where collaboration is open, and we’re excited to help steward OpenShell alongside NVIDIA and the broader ecosystem.”

— Chris Wright, Chief Technology Officer and Senior Vice President of Global Engineering, Red Hat

Contributing OpenShell to the CNCF as a neutral foundation is a natural next step to expand and grow the OpenShell project. It has adopted the CNCF Code of Conduct, runs a public RFC process, and follows a governance model with explicit vendor-neutrality commitments. By contributing OpenShell alongside partners and maintainers from across the industry, NVIDIA aims to make secure AI available to all, under the same open governance model that supports other CNCF projects.

Built for an ecosystem

No two organizations run agents the same way. They use different infrastructure, secret stores, inference providers, and governance practices, and those choices change over time. OpenShell is designed to fit this variety through well-defined extension points for providers, compute, governance and approval workflows, policy enforcement, isolation, and credential management. Teams can adopt it incrementally and swap in what they already run. It also gives vendors, integrators, and end users clear places to contribute.

What changes, and what doesn’t

OpenShell is moving from NVIDIA’s GitHub repository to a neutral organization, ai-openshell. Working groups and special interest groups will form around integrated components and cross-cutting topics such as observability.

The core engineering efforts from NVIDIA will continue, while we welcome contributions from other interested parties.

Ways to participate

Whether your organization already uses OpenShell or is just exploring it, contributing is the best way to shape its future. Areas where help is especially welcome include:

  • Extension implementations. Reference implementations for compute, credential management, inference, and logging, along with shared documentation and conformance tests so third-party integrations behave consistently.
  • Policy and governance patterns. Real-world approval flows, egress rules, and per-tenant policies, shared as examples or a policy library, plus feedback on the Cedar-based policy approach.
  • Isolation and platform coverage. Broader support across Linux, macOS, and Kubernetes, security reviews, adversarial testing, and vendor-neutral confidential computing work.
  • Observability. Consistent metrics, traces, and audit events aligned with OpenTelemetry.
  • Packaging and release engineering. Package maintenance, reproducible builds, SBOMs, signing, and CI, all of which support Incubation requirements.
  • Deployment at scale. Multi-tenancy, identity and access integration, and policy management workflows drawn from your own deployments.

Get involved

  • Join the community mailing list for notes and call invitations.
  • Find the project in the CNCF Slack channel #openshell-dev.
  • Watch the ai-openshell GitHub organization for new repositories, “good first issue” labels, and design proposals.

Contributors, end users, and people who are both are welcome. We look forward to building the future of open agent governance together.

title: 香港按揭证券有限公司与亚洲基础设施投资银行签署合作意向书
summary: 香港按揭证券有限公司与亚洲基础设施投资银行签署合作意向书，正式建立合作关系。该合作消息由香港金融管理局以新闻稿形式对外发布。
context: 香港按揭融资平台与多边开发银行携手，债务融资与基础设施投资领域的合作动向值得关注。
contentHtml:
香港按揭证券有限公司（按揭证券公司）与亚洲基础设施投资银行（亚投行）已于11月20日在香港签署合作意向书，确立双方的合作框架。

在是次签署的意向书之下，双方计划在多个方面加强合作，如发掘可持续基建领域的潜在联合融资机会、将相关气候变化战略融入基建投资、培养可持续基建融资人才、开展数码工具方面的交流及深化在基建贷款抵押证券发行方面的合作，实践双方加强将私有资本引入基建领域的共同目标。

在过去三年，亚投行透过其总计三亿美元的投资计划 Project Ocean，作为锚定投资者支持按揭证券公司基建贷款抵押证券的发行，并主要投资于其中的可持续融资票据。

按揭证券公司为履行促进本地债券市场发展的使命，于过去三年致力透过定期发行Bauhinia系列之基建贷款抵押证券（Bauhinia系列证券），以期达致推广此类证券作为独立资产类别的长远目标，巩固香港作为基建融资中心的地位。Bauhinia系列证券的发行为专业投资者提供一个投资横跨不同地域和行业的多元化项目和基建债务机会。亚投行作为Bauhinia系列票据发行的积极投资者，其多边开发银行的地位和参与度提升了投资者的信心，进一步扩大投资者基础和促进私有资本的流动性。

按揭证券公司执行董事兼总裁鲍克运表示：「随著按揭证券公司的基建融资及证券化平台业务在过往几年的显著增长，我们希望加强与我们网络内的金融机构、商业银行和多边开发银行的合作。我们进一步深化与亚投行的合作，将为推进我们的业务带来更多机遇，并促进香港作为基建融资中心的发展。」

亚投行公共部门（第一区）金融机构及基金客户（全球）首席投资官林金思表示：「亚投行很高兴能够拓展与按揭证券公司的合作。我们期待运用双方在基建融资领域的专长，并通过支持基建贷款抵押证券的持续发展，动员私有资本进入新兴市场基础设施项目​​的投资。」

香港按揭证券有限公司
2026年11月23日


香港按揭证券有限公司执行董事兼总裁鲍克运（左）和亚洲基础设施投资银行公共部门（第一区）金融机构及基金客户（全球）首席投资官林金思（右）签署合作意向书，正式确立双方合作框架。


香港按揭证券有限公司执行董事兼总裁鲍克运（左二）和亚洲基础设施投资银行公共部门（第一区）金融机构及基金客户（全球）首席投资官林金思（右二）继签署合作意向书后，连同按揭证券公司首席投资总监（基建融资及证券化产品）郑文信（左一）和亚投行金融机构及基金客户（全球）资深投资官Torsten Albrecht（右一）参与祝酒仪式。
