summary: AWS 推出 SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway，通过一个托管端点即可在单区域或多区域的 HyperPod 集群间路由推理请求。该网关自动选择最优集群并支持故障自动转移，所有请求经 AWS PrivateLink 使用 SigV4 与 IAM 完成认证。
context: 跨区域推理路由与容灾一直是大规模模型服务难点，该能力显著降低多集群推理的运维复杂度。
originalTitle: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: One endpoint across Regions and clusters
author: Dmitry Soldatkin
contentHtml:
During a traffic peak, a request can sit in a queue on a saturated HyperPod cluster while GPUs on another cluster, sometimes in another AWS Region, sit idle. You have already paid for that capacity, but your requests can’t reach it.

In Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway, we showed how the Inference Gateway gives each Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster a single, GPU-aware endpoint. It reads real-time signals such as key-value (KV) cache utilization and queue depth to place every request on the best-suited pod. That solves routing inside one cluster, but not across clusters.

Today, SageMaker HyperPod introduces the Global Inference Gateway. It is one SageMaker-managed gateway that routes across every cluster you register, in one Region or across Regions. The gateway picks the cluster and carries the request over the AWS backbone, with automatic failover and authentication through AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Inside each cluster, the Inference Gateway keeps picking the pod, unchanged. The Global Inference Gateway is the second tier of the architecture we described in part 1.

The challenge: Capacity spread across clusters and Regions

Models are getting larger, and the GPU capacity to serve them is harder to find. To get enough of it, you spread it across more clusters and more Regions.

Consider a team that serves four models across five HyperPod clusters in two Regions. Without the Inference Gateway, clients track 20 endpoints: one per model per cluster. The Inference Gateway cuts that to five, one per cluster. But each client still picks a cluster itself.

That choice has costs:

  • Uneven load. During peaks, requests queue in one Region while GPUs in the other Region are idle.
  • Manual failover. When a cluster fails, an engineer changes configuration to move traffic away from it.
  • Custom plumbing. Spreading traffic across Regions means building and maintaining load balancers, DNS, and cross-Region networking yourself.

The team needs one endpoint that sends each request to the best-suited cluster and moves traffic off a failed cluster on its own.

Key benefits

The Global Inference Gateway helps you get more from the GPU capacity you already have, with less to operate.

  • Put idle GPUs to work. During a peak, requests overflow to clusters with available capacity in the same Region or another one, instead of queuing on a saturated cluster.
  • Fail over automatically. When a cluster fails, the gateway moves its traffic to the next-best cluster. Clients don’t change anything.
  • Use one endpoint for everything. Clients call a single SageMaker-managed endpoint instead of tracking one endpoint per cluster or per model.
  • Skip the custom networking. You don’t build or maintain load balancers, DNS, or cross-Region networking.
  • Stay private by default. Every request is authenticated with SigV4 and IAM, and it reaches your clusters only over AWS PrivateLink.

Customer feedback

“At Bagelcode, we run our own LLM inference service on AWS to help teams across the company, including our game teams, use AI to improve how they work. In our beta tests, the Global Inference Gateway in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod routed requests across two AWS Regions through a single endpoint and kept serving them when one cluster could no longer serve the model. That gave our small platform team cross-Region failover without having to build or maintain our own routing layer.”

— Jinhyung Park, VP (AI Platform), Bagelcode

How it works

Setting up the gateway takes two decisions: which clusters to open up for routing, and which of them to group behind one gateway.

  1. Publish a cluster. You do this once per cluster. You turn on the spec.globalRouting block in the cluster’s existing InferenceGatewayConfig. The HyperPod Inference controller then publishes the cluster privately from your own account.
  2. Create the gateway. You do this once per gateway. You call CreateGlobalInferenceGateway with the clusters to route across, and SageMaker returns one endpoint.

A cluster is reachable only after you publish it. When you publish a cluster, the controller creates a Network Load Balancer in front of the cluster’s Inference Gateway, publishes a virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint service on it, and uploads the listener’s certificate to your TLS bucket. These resources live in your account. If you list a cluster in a gateway before you publish it, the call fails with a message that tells you what to fix.

How a request flows

Figure 1 shows the path of each request: (1) your client signs the request with SigV4 and sends it to the gateway’s regional endpoint. (2) The gateway authenticates the caller and picks the best cluster. (3) AWS PrivateLink carries the request to that cluster, in the same Region or another, and (4) the cluster’s Inference Gateway routes it to a model pod, as it does today.

Figure 1: The Global Inference Gateway receives each request at one regional endpoint and forwards it over AWS PrivateLink to the best HyperPod cluster, where the cluster’s Inference Gateway routes it to a model pod. Each cluster publishes its load back to the gateway.

What AWS operates

You decide which clusters to publish, which to group behind a gateway, and how to weight routing. AWS operates the rest:

  • The routing fleet. SageMaker provisions and operates the fleet that terminates TLS, authenticates callers, scores clusters, and forwards each request.
  • Private connectivity. SageMaker creates one private endpoint per cluster and carries traffic on the AWS backbone, in-Region and cross-Region.
  • Certificates and validation. Using an execution role that you create, the service reads each cluster’s VPC endpoint service name, certificate, and Region, so you don’t copy them by hand. It checks them before routing traffic.
  • Health and failover. The gateway health-checks every cluster and moves traffic off a failed cluster automatically. For details, see the Operating the gateway section.
  • Authentication and rate limits. The gateway checks SigV4 signatures, IAM permissions, and rate limits, and rejects failing requests before any cluster sees them.

On each cluster, a service-managed metrics publisher with its own IAM role sends the cluster’s load to the gateway.

How the gateway picks a cluster

For each request, the gateway scores every healthy cluster on four signals and sends the request to the highest-scoring cluster. Each cluster’s metrics publisher supplies the load signals.

You control how much each signal counts with routing weights. Each weight is a value from 0.0 to 1.0, and a weight of 0 turns that signal off. If you set weights, you set all four, and they must add up to 1.0. If you omit them, the defaults in the following table apply.

Weight What it scores Default
KVHeadroom Available KV cache and GPU memory on the cluster 0.20
QueueDepth How backed up the cluster is 0.25
RegionProximity Distance between the cluster and the gateway’s Region 0.40
ErrorRate Recent failed requests on the cluster 0.15

The defaults favor clusters close to the gateway’s Region, while still moving traffic toward clusters with available capacity and away from clusters that are failing. If resilience matters more than proximity for your workload, raise ErrorRate and lower RegionProximity. For example, the following routing block weights recent errors at 0.7:

{"Weights": {"KVHeadroom": 0.1, "QueueDepth": 0.1, "RegionProximity": 0.1, "ErrorRate": 0.7}}

You pass the weights in the Routing parameter of CreateGlobalInferenceGateway, and you can change them later with UpdateGlobalInferenceGateway.

Choose your starting point

Your path depends on what you run today. If you serve from a single cluster, stay on that cluster’s Inference Gateway endpoint. Move to the Global Inference Gateway when you add a second cluster.

Starting point What you do Result
The Inference Gateway runs on each cluster, for example four models on five clusters in us-east-1 and us-west-2 Update the add-on, publish each cluster, and create the gateway One endpoint for every cluster. Per-cluster endpoints keep serving while you move clients over.
The HyperPod Inference add-on runs with the Inference Gateway turned off Turn on the Inference Gateway with one add-on update and one InferenceGatewayConfig per cluster, add a scheduler for each model, then follow the first row Per-model endpoints collapse into one
GPU capacity in two Regions, but no HyperPod Inference setup yet Create a HyperPod cluster in each Region with the HyperPod Inference add-on, deploy your model, turn on the Inference Gateway, then follow the first row One endpoint from day one, with traffic whose routing can be fine-tuned, and keeps serving if a Region has a problem

Getting started

To set up the Global Inference Gateway, you prepare each cluster, create an execution role, and call CreateGlobalInferenceGateway. You then send OpenAI-compatible requests, signed with SigV4, to the gateway endpoint. For step-by-step instructions, including the IAM roles and policies, see the AWS documentation.

Security and access

Every request to the gateway is signed with SigV4 and authorized with IAM. Callers need permission to invoke the gateway, and streaming has its own action:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": [
      "sagemaker:InvokeGlobalInferenceGateway",
      "sagemaker:InvokeGlobalInferenceGatewayWithResponseStream"
    ],
    "Resource": "arn:aws:sagemaker:<region>:<account-id>:global-inference-gateway/<gateway-id>"
  }]
}

Attach this policy to each IAM identity that sends requests. To allow every gateway in the account, use global-inference-gateway/* as the resource.

The execution role follows least privilege. It can describe only the clusters you list, reach only their Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) API, and read only the routing certificates under the gig/ prefix of your TLS bucket, tagged as created by HyperPod Inference.

Identity tokens. If your clusters check JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), pass the token with --customer-identity-token (the X-Amzn-SageMaker-Customer-Identity-Token header), with no Bearer prefix. The token travels inside the SigV4 signature, so an unsigned token is rejected with 403 and a repeated token with 400. Turn on JWT checks on every cluster that serves a model, or on none of them, so a request doesn’t succeed on one cluster and fail on another.

Requests reach your clusters only through AWS PrivateLink, as shown in Figure 1. The gateway does not log or store prompts or completions.

Operating the gateway

Here are steps to configure the gateway.

Add a cluster

Prepare the new cluster and create the execution role’s EKS access entry on it, as described in the documentation. Also add the new cluster to the Resource lists of the execution role’s permissions policy. Then call AddInferenceGateway in the gateway’s Region, even if the new cluster is in another Region:

aws sagemaker add-inference-gateway \
  --identifier <gateway-name> \
  --region <region> \
  --cluster-arn arn:aws:sagemaker:<region-3>:<account-id>:cluster/<cluster-id-3> \
  --name <gateway-config-name-3> \
  --namespace inference-gateway

The gateway validates the cluster and starts routing to it once it is healthy. The endpoint, other clusters, and clients aren’t affected.

Detach a cluster

Call RemoveInferenceGateway in the gateway’s Region:

aws sagemaker remove-inference-gateway \
  --identifier <gateway-name> \
  --region <region> \
  --cluster-arn arn:aws:sagemaker:<region-3>:<account-id>:cluster/<cluster-id-3> \
  --name <gateway-config-name-3> \
  --namespace inference-gateway

The gateway stops sending new requests to the cluster, lets in-flight requests finish, and removes the private endpoint. A gateway always keeps at least one cluster. To withdraw the cluster fully, set globalRouting.enabled: false in its InferenceGatewayConfig and reapply it.

Delete the gateway

Call DeleteGlobalInferenceGateway:

aws sagemaker delete-global-inference-gateway \
  --identifier <gateway-name> --region <region>

The gateway endpoint stops serving, and per-cluster endpoints keep serving. After the gateway is deleted, withdraw each cluster with globalRouting.enabled: false, then delete the execution role and the IAM permissions you added for global routing.

The following table summarizes how common events and changes affect traffic.

Event What happens What you do
Gateway creation fails The gateway moves to FAILED, and FailureReason says what failed, such as a certificate name mismatch Fix the cause. To see each cluster’s status, call ListInferenceGateways.
A cluster fails Traffic moves to the next-best cluster, and the cluster returns gradually after it recovers. A failed request is retried once on another cluster unless it has started streaming. If no healthy cluster is left, the gateway returns 503. Nothing. Clients don’t change anything.
Change routing weights New requests use the new weights, and in-flight requests finish under the old ones. Nothing is re-provisioned. Call UpdateGlobalInferenceGateway
Add a cluster Routing starts once the cluster is healthy. Nothing else changes. See Add a cluster
Detach a cluster New requests stop, and in-flight requests finish See Detach a cluster
Delete the gateway The gateway endpoint stops serving, and per-cluster endpoints keep serving See Delete the gateway

For any troubleshooting assistance, please see the Troubleshooting Guide.

Best practices and considerations

  • Plan your groups before you publish. Decide which clusters sit behind each gateway, with the same modelName on every cluster that should share a model’s traffic. If you want peak traffic to overflow across Regions, give clusters in both Regions headroom.
  • Publish only the clusters you add to a gateway. A published cluster that isn’t in any gateway receives no traffic, but its Network Load Balancer still runs and is billed.
  • Cover every model. Each scheduler in the InferenceGatewayConfig maps a model name to the pods that serve it. A model that isn’t in any scheduler can’t be reached through the gateway, and requests for it return a 404 error.
  • Keep your add-on configuration complete. With --resolve-conflicts OVERWRITE, an incomplete configuration can reset your load balancer or TLS settings. Start from the current configuration every time.
  • Pass --context on every kubectl command. You work across several clusters, so make sure each command runs against the cluster you mean.
  • Keep a workload in one Region when you need to. Create a gateway that includes only clusters in that Region.

Conclusion

In this post, we introduced the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: one SageMaker-managed endpoint across your HyperPod clusters, in one Region or several. The gateway picks the cluster based on KV cache headroom, queue depth, Region proximity, and error rate, and moves traffic off a failed cluster with no client changes.

The Global Inference Gateway is available in 13 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Singapore), and Asia Pacific (Sydney).

To get started, see the AWS documentation.

originalTitle: How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI
author: Tala Qraitem
contentHtml:
This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group

Having an AI policy is one thing. Proving, one use case at a time, that AI systems follow it is another. Every new generative AI application adds one more system to prove. Teams can now build one in days, but each still needs a risk committee’s approval before it reaches customers or employees. When that approval depends on reviewers reading documents and testing the system by hand, governance becomes the slowest step in the pipeline.

Standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof. Working with AWS Professional Services, the bank deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard that show what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. This post explains how the assessment runs on AWS and what Standard Bank Group learned from its first runs.

Governing AI with the framework you already have

Standard Bank Group didn’t need a new AI policy. Like most large banks, it already had an established model risk practice that covers concerns such as explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case according to its level of risk before it goes live.

Generative AI increases the complexity, because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case still needs to meet the same high security and compliance bar.

“At Standard Bank, this assessment demonstrates how we are working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into our AI journey, allowing us to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. We believe responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence.”

— Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer, Standard Bank Group

The goal was to automate evidence gathering and testing, then feed the results into the approval gates Standard Bank Group already runs. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, but the committee now bases each decision on consistent evidence, collected the same way across use cases.

How the assessment works

Figure 1 shows how the assessment’s components fit together in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting.

Figure 1: The assessment pipeline in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting

The assessment runs entirely in Standard Bank Group’s own AWS account. Documents, code, and test results stay in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket there. The AWS Well-Architected Tool handles intake, AWS Step Functions orchestrates the pipeline, and a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock evaluates the evidence. It uses a technique called LLM-as-a-judge, in which a large language model checks evidence against defined criteria.

With Amazon Bedrock, Standard Bank Group could use a foundation model without stepping outside the controls it already runs on AWS. The bank controls access to the model through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), just as it does for its other AWS workloads. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t share the bank’s prompts or model outputs with model providers, and doesn’t use them to train models. Because Amazon Bedrock offers many foundation models through one API, the team can move to a newer judge model by changing a configuration setting instead of rebuilding the pipeline.

Each assessment moves through four steps. In the first two, a pre-assessment agent collects evidence about the use case, then the pipeline examines it and tests the application directly. The third evaluates that evidence against controls. The fourth summarizes the results in a standard, predefined format and delivers them to the people who act on them.

Step 1: A pre-assessment agent collects the evidence

The custom lens in the Well-Architected Tool holds about 40 questions, each covering a risk event such as incomplete technical documentation or insufficient human oversight. Delivery teams no longer fill it in from scratch. A pre-assessment agent running on AWS Fargate scans the use case’s code repository and documentation. It maps relevant files to each question and pre-populates the lens with answers and links to the evidence. The delivery team then reviews those answers, corrects any mistakes, and adds the evidence the agent couldn’t find.

Step 2: The pipeline examines the artifacts and tests the application

The pipeline works from four kinds of evidence.

  • System documentation, which describes how the application was designed, built, and evaluated.
  • Policy documents, which set out roles, responsibilities, and procedures such as incident handling.
  • Source code and the system prompt, which show how controls are implemented.
  • Live calls to the application, which show how it behaves in practice.

For documents and code, the pipeline checks whether each artifact contains what its mapped control requires. Each control comes from an international AI standard or framework, or from Standard Bank Group’s own policies. An incident procedure, for example, needs to describe how incidents are reported.

For live testing, the pipeline calls the application through its AWS Lambda function or API. The delivery team supplies questions a typical user would ask. The pipeline adds a built-in set of jailbreak attempts and off-topic questions, which the application is expected to decline. It also sends the same prompt several times, in its original and reworded forms, and uses an embedding model on Amazon Bedrock to check that the answers stay consistent in meaning. Where the team provides expected answers, the pipeline measures how closely the responses match them. Every response is stored in Amazon S3, so reviewers can see exactly what the application generated.

Step 3: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation against standards

In this step, a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock acts as the judge. The assessment uses the model as-is with no fine-tuning or customization. (Model availability varies by AWS Region, so check the supported models by Region before you deploy.) For each question, the model checks whether specific evidence appears in the artifacts and in the application’s responses, and returns yes or no.

Every check maps to a control in an international standard or framework for AI management, AI risk, or AI security. Standard Bank Group also customized the lens with judge questions built from its own standards, bringing the total to more than 300. The checks cover the eight AWS responsible AI dimensions in the following table:

Dimension What the assessment looks for
Veracity and robustness Correct outputs, even with unexpected or adversarial inputs
Privacy and security Appropriate collection, use, and protection of data and models
Transparency Information that helps stakeholders make informed choices about their use of an AI system
Fairness Consideration of impacts on different groups of stakeholders
Safety Prevention of harmful output and misuse
Controllability Mechanisms to monitor and steer system behavior
Governance Best practices across the AI supply chain, including providers and deployers
Explainability Ways to understand and evaluate system outputs

Each risk receives a likelihood score, the share of required evidence the model couldn’t find, and a fixed severity level that the bank’s risk team can adjust. Together they produce a rating from Very low to Critical. Each missing piece of evidence maps to a specific mitigation and to the clause of the standard or policy it came from. A risk officer can then trace any findings back to their source when explaining decisions to a regulator. Figure 2 follows one missing piece of evidence through this process, from the evidence request to the recommended fix.

Figure 2: How one finding is traced from evidence to fix

Standard Bank Group protects and checks the assessment’s output in two ways. Every AI model interaction is protected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, ensuring alignment with the bank’s established security and responsible AI standards. The assessment’s model calls pass through the same safeguards the bank enforces across its AWS accounts for its AI workloads. These guardrails screen for harmful content and for attempts to manipulate the model.

The assessment is also designed so its output can be checked. Instead of asking the model for an open-ended opinion, the pipeline asks narrow yes-or-no questions, each worded to match a specific control. A fixed formula that the risk team can inspect turns those answers into scores. Each evaluation runs multiple times to measure how consistent the answers are and any inconsistent findings are flagged in the review interface. Every judgment is stored with the evidence behind it so that reviewers and auditors can trace how it was reached.

Step 4: Reports for each audience

The pipeline summarizes the results in a standard format and delivers them as an executive presentation, a mitigation checklist, a detailed technical report, and an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that tracks scores across use cases over time. Before a gate decision, reviewers confirm findings in a custom review interface with single sign-on. There they can add the use case, review the questions, amend answers with a business justification, and rewrite the output.

The assessment produces evidence against controls. It doesn’t certify compliance with any regulation, and Standard Bank Group remains responsible for its own regulatory determinations.

Testing against Standard Bank Group’s own rules

International standards give every use case a common baseline, but the bank’s risk committees approve use cases against its own policy. A question factory addresses this by generating extra judge questions from internal documents. Standard Bank Group’s risk team used it to turn internal policies into checks that run on every use case.

Because those checks are derived directly from policy language, a policy change becomes a test change. Every subsequent assessment applies the updated rule automatically, with minimal manual rework by the risk team.

“Most organizations treat policy as something you read. Standard Bank Group treats it as something you run. When every rule becomes a check that runs against the live system, a policy update stops being a memo and becomes a test. That fundamentally changes how fast a bank can scale AI responsibly.”

— Sri Elaprolu, Director, Frontier AI Science & Engineering, AWS

Built into the use case lifecycle

The assessment fits into three stages of the use case lifecycle. During a proof of concept, it is optional, giving teams an early view of potential gaps. At the build stage, it becomes mandatory, and the approval gate draws on its results as formal evidence. Today the assessment runs in Standard Bank Group’s production environment, evaluating use cases before they go live. After live workloads are connected, the assessment will rerun on a schedule or whenever code or configuration changes, keeping the evidence current well beyond launch. The bank’s teams already trigger assessments on their own through a central system where use cases flow from intake to evaluation in a single workflow.

What this means for financial institutions

At Standard Bank Group, the assessment reduced a traditionally manual two-week review to a comprehensive risk report generated in approximately two hours, demonstrated across six assessments. It also delivered a 14% improvement in use-case risk scores after remediation. This strengthens responsible AI governance, reduces compliance bottlenecks, and shortens the path from assessment to production.

This approach can benefit three groups involved in approving AI use cases:

  • Risk and compliance leaders get evidence in the same format for every use case, traceable to a published standard or an internal policy clause. Start from the framework you already run, as Standard Bank Group did with its existing risk processes and approval gates.
  • Delivery teams learn what to fix during the proof of concept, when changes cost the least, instead of meeting a rejection at the approval gate.
  • Executives can grow the AI portfolio without growing the review effort at the same rate.

“Adoption of AI at scale across the enterprise requires trust, both internally and with our customers. This assessment is proving key in enabling all our product teams to demonstrate that they are building enterprise-grade solutions aligned with both our own and industry best practices.”

— Duncan Macdonald, Chief Technology Officer, Standard Bank Group

From approval gates to continuous assurance

Banks designed approval gates for systems that changed a few times a year. Generative AI applications change with every prompt update, model version, and new data source. As they take on more autonomous tasks, the number of decisions that need evidence keeps growing. Adding reviewers can’t keep pace with that rate of change.

Standard Bank Group’s approach points to a different operating model. When policies become tests and evidence is collected automatically, governance moves out of a checkpoint at the end of delivery and into the system itself. Every AI application in the portfolio can carry a current, auditable record of how it meets the bank’s standards, refreshed whenever its code or configuration changes. Risk teams spend their time on judgment calls and policy design, and the bank can show regulators the same evidence it uses for its own decisions.

The same foundation extends further. Continuous reassessment keeps evidence aligned with a changing code base after launch. New regulations can be encoded once as checks and applied across every use case. Aggregated scores give boards an enterprise-wide view of AI risk instead of a collection of individual reviews.

For any institution scaling AI, the question worth asking is how many of its policies have ever been tested against a running system. To explore how AWS Professional Services can help your organization automate AI risk assessment, contact your AWS account team. To learn more about building AI responsibly on AWS, visit Responsible AI on AWS.

title: Cloudflare WAF 如何防护 ruby2shell（CVE-2026-132825）漏洞
originalTitle: How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)
author: Daniele Molteni
summary: Cloudflare WAF 已面向全部客户（含 Free 免费版）开启对 ruby2shell（CVE-2026-132825）攻击的拦截。该漏洞允许攻击者在无需登录的情况下破坏默认配置的 Rails 和 Sinatra 应用内存。官方建议尽快升级 Ruby，并利用 WAF 覆盖升级前的风险空窗期。
context: 无需认证即可利用、默认配置即受影响，该漏洞对 Rails/Sinatra 用户构成直接威胁。
contentHtml:
On November 19, 2026, the Ruby team disclosed ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825), a heap buffer overflow in the way Ruby changes the case of strings. Ruby rates the flaw Critical and says it is aware of proofs of concept that achieve remote code execution in some scenarios. Fixes shipped in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10.

The reach is wide. Veria Labs reports that Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications reach the bug in their default configuration, before any authentication. Self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse and Chatwoot, shipped an affected Ruby in their latest release at the time of disclosure.

Cloudflare WAF blocks ruby2shell for all customers, including those on the Free plan. We have added two rules to both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, with Block as the default action: one for ruby2shell and one for GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a related integer overflow in Ruby string case conversion fixed in the same releases.

The WAF is a compensating control, not a replacement for patching. Exploits can reach the bug through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade Ruby. Our team continues to monitor attack traffic and will update the rules as new techniques appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get the latest on the vulnerability in the Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.

Cloudflare has patched its own systems that use Ruby, and we have found no indication of compromise.

What we know about ruby2shell

Ruby strings carry an encoding, and Ruby still supports many legacy single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) and Windows-1252, alongside UTF-8. In a single-byte encoding each character takes one byte, so changing the case of a string usually produces output of the same length.

The German sharp s (ß) breaks that assumption. Its uppercase form is two characters, SS. In 14 ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings, Ruby writes those two bytes but checks for room for only one. According to Veria Labs, a string with 21 sharp s characters overflows the output buffer by one byte. The methods that reach the bug are upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

A one-byte overflow can look harmless. In a memory-corruption exploit, though, a single byte written past the end of a heap buffer can be enough to corrupt an adjacent object or allocator metadata. Ruby says it is aware of proofs of concept that turn this flaw into code execution, and Veria Labs says it will publish its own proof of concept about a week after disclosure. We expect scanning to start soon after.

Why default Rails and Sinatra apps are exposed

HTML forms can only send GET and POST requests. To simulate PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, many web frameworks accept a _method parameter in a POST request. Rack, the interface most Ruby web frameworks build on, implements this in its MethodOverride middleware, which converts the value of _method to uppercase. Rails includes this middleware by default, and classic-style Sinatra applications enable it. An attacker can send a multipart POST request whose _method part declares a legacy character set and contains a run of sharp s characters. The framework upcases the value while it is still routing the request, before any application code or authentication check runs.

Veria Labs reports that other frameworks and plain Rack applications are not exposed by default. Application code that changes the case of strings received in a legacy encoding may still be affected, wherever the string comes from.

Who is affected

Condition

Details

Ruby version

Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Veria Labs reports the bug has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix.

Framework

Rails and classic-style Sinatra in their default configuration. Any other code that changes the case of attacker-controlled strings in a legacy single-byte encoding.

Bundled software

As of November 19, 2026, Veria Labs lists GitLab 19.6.0, GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5, Mastodon 4.7.5, OpenProject 17.9.7, Discourse 2026.10.1 and Chatwoot 4.20.0 as bundling an affected Ruby in their latest release. Discourse moved its Docker base image to Ruby 4.0.10 on November 19, so rebuilding a Docker install picks up the fix.

Distribution packages can backport fixes without changing the Ruby version number, so check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.

Six more Ruby flaws in the same release

Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 also fix six other memory safety flaws, and Ruby says several of them can lead to code execution. One, GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, is an integer overflow in the same string case conversion code, and our second WAF rule covers it. The other five are in Ruby's regular expression engine. Most of them require the application to compile or match a regular expression pattern supplied by the attacker. That is uncommon in web applications, but it does happen in search features, filtering rules and admin tools.

How Cloudflare WAF protects you

Upgrading every Ruby runtime takes time, especially when Ruby is bundled inside self-hosted products and container images. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch.

New managed rules, on for every customer

Both rules are part of the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee), with Block as the default action.

Rule description

Ruleset

Default action

On the Free plan, the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset runs automatically, so there is nothing to turn on. On paid plans, the rules are active wherever the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed. Because paid plans give you more control over how rulesets are deployed, the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset may not be active on every zone. We recommend checking its status to confirm that it is running. You can use the links in the Zero Wire briefing to go straight to the rules in your dashboard.

What the WAF cannot see

A WAF can block an exploit when the malicious input arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable code:

  • Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. Requests sent directly to your origin IP address, and traffic between internal services, never reach the WAF. Configure your origin to accept traffic only from Cloudflare, for example with Cloudflare Tunnel or Authenticated Origin Pulls.
  • Other entry points into the same code. Ruby code that changes the case of strings from email, file imports, message queues or background jobs can reach ruby2shell without an HTTP request.

Adding defense in depth with WAF attack score

Memory corruption is usually only the first step. To run commands, an attacker still has to deliver a second-stage payload, such as shell commands or a reverse shell, and then interact with the compromised server. WAF attack score uses machine learning to score each request for remote code execution payloads, which helps catch exploit variations and post-exploitation traffic that signature-based rules can miss. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans.

Impact on Cloudflare infrastructure

Cloudflare has patched its systems that use Ruby against ruby2shell. We have found no indication of compromise and continue to monitor.

Patch now

ruby2shell turns a one-byte miscalculation in string case conversion into a pre-authentication path to code execution in default Rails and Sinatra apps. With a public proof of concept expected within days, the window to patch is short. Here is what to do:

  1. Check your WAF coverage. On the Free plan, the ruby2shell rules are already blocking. On paid plans, confirm the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and the rules have not been overridden.
  2. Upgrade Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10 and restart every Ruby process, including background workers. Rebuild container images. Move applications on Ruby 3.2 or earlier to a supported series.
  3. Update self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject and Chatwoot, as each vendor releases a fix. Rebuild Discourse Docker installs now.
  4. Inventory your runtimes. The Zero Wire briefing includes a prompt you can give an AI agent to find every affected Ruby runtime in your infrastructure.

Our WAF analysts will keep updating protections as new techniques appear. Follow the WAF changelog for rule updates.

title: Cloudflare WAF 如何防护 phpAfterShell 及其他严重 PHP 漏洞
originalTitle: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against phpAfterShell and other critical PHP flaws
author: Daniele Molteni
summary: Cloudflare WAF 已可拦截 PHP 默认 session 处理器中的严重漏洞 phpAfterShell，该漏洞可导致代码执行，防护覆盖包括 Free 套餐在内的所有客户。Cloudflare 同时新增规则，拦截同一版本修复的其他 PHP 漏洞。
context: PHP 使用极为广泛，默认组件中出现可代码执行的严重漏洞影响面大，WAF 防护对所有套餐默认生效值得关注。
contentHtml:
On November 19, 2026, the security research company depthfirst disclosed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a vulnerability in PHP's default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The PHP project fixed it the same day in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, and 8.6.0. These releases fix 16 other security vulnerabilities, six of them also rated critical.

Cloudflare’s web application firewall (WAF) blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns, including for customers on the Free plan. The protection comes from a PHP remote code execution rule we first deployed in October 2026 for the php2shell vulnerabilities. That rule already detected part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before the vulnerability was disclosed, and on November 19 we updated its detection logic to cover phpAfterShell. The rule is part of both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, is enabled by default, and its default action is Block.

In the same WAF release, we added three new rules to the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset for paid plans: one for a request smuggling flaw in PHP-FPM (CVE-2026-129289), and two for flaws in PHP's SOAP extension (CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506) that PHP fixed in the same releases. These rules are enabled by default with the Log action, because the request patterns they look for can also appear in legitimate traffic, and blocking by default could disrupt it. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the action to Block once they confirm the rules do not affect legitimate traffic.

The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Several of the critical flaws depend on server configuration or can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade PHP and restart every worker. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and follow how the vulnerabilities develop in the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.

There appears to be no indication so far that these vulnerabilities have been exploited. As of November 19, 2026, none of the 17 vulnerabilities was listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no source we reviewed reports exploitation in the wild.

What we know about phpAfterShell

PHP stores session data in files by default. When an application calls session_start(), PHP reads the session file and deserializes its content into the $_SESSION array. When the request ends, PHP writes the updated session back to the same file.

phpAfterShell is triggered when that write is interrupted. The session file can then hold the beginning of the new session data followed by the end of the old one. On the next request, session_start() deserializes this mixed content. If an attacker controlled the old data, PHP can end up deserializing objects of the attacker's choice.

An attacker trying to exploit the flaw is likely to first search for a way to place controlled data in the session. PHP's advisory names two:

  • Session upload progress, a PHP feature that writes information about a running file upload into the session. A remote client can use it to shape the stored data.
  • Applications that store large user-controlled strings in the session.

According to PHP, code execution also requires an interruption at a useful point in the write and a suitable deserialization gadget chain in the application. depthfirst reports that it reached code execution without an application gadget by chaining a second, undisclosed memory-corruption bug in a PHP-native class. The sources we reviewed do not establish whether that second bug is fixed in the November 19 releases.

depthfirst says it discovered and reported phpAfterShell. The CVE record credits Leo Lin and Asahi as reporters.

The other critical flaws

The same releases fix six more critical vulnerabilities. Each one needs a specific configuration to be exploitable:

CVE

Component

Impact

Conditions

CVE-2026-129289

PHP-FPM

An unauthenticated attacker can smuggle a second FastCGI request into PHP-FPM and run PHP code as the worker.

A front end that reuses backend FastCGI connections (nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, or HAProxy), an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end, and the path of an existing PHP script.

CVE-2026-115560

Session serializer

Object injection through a mismatch between session serializers. First covered in our php2shell briefing, now fixed.

Session upload progress enabled. PHP widened the scope: applications, pools or command-line jobs that use different serializers and share a session store are affected.

CVE-2026-129496

Timezone cache

Use-after-free that can crash a fresh worker and possibly run code. PHP demonstrated code execution locally with known memory addresses.

Non-thread-safe builds where a startup diagnostic has been written to a PHP error log file.

CVE-2026-129481

Session shutdown

Use-after-free, described by PHP as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619. No code execution demonstrated.

PHP 8.3 and later.

CVE-2026-129474

Fatal error backtraces

Use-after-free in magic method backtraces.

PHP 8.5 and later, where fatal error backtraces are enabled by default. Setting zend.exception_ignore_args=1, the php.ini-production default, blocks the demonstrated attack.

CVE-2026-129182

Fatal error backtraces

Use-after-free. No code execution demonstrated.

PHP 8.5, specific path-level settings, and an Apache per-directory configuration or front end that produces an early diagnostic.

Who is affected

The vulnerable versions are PHP 8.2 before 8.2.36, 8.3 before 8.3.37, 8.4 before 8.4.28, 8.5 before 8.5.13, and the 8.6.0 release candidates. Whether a deployment is exposed depends on the conditions of each flaw.

PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life. depthfirst says the official 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 end-of-life mitigation branches are not affected by phpAfterShell, but PHP says CVE-2026-129289 was introduced in PHP 5.6.0 and that releases older than 8.2 may also be affected by CVE-2026-115560.

Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the PHP version number. Check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.

How Cloudflare WAF protects you

PHP runs a large share of the web, often inside content management systems, plugins, and container images that teams do not update directly. Patching every PHP runtime takes time. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch.

phpAfterShell: protection on every plan

We released the original PHP remote code execution rules in an emergency release on October 21, 2026, after the php2shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) were disclosed. We extended them to CVE-2026-115560 on October 23 and refined them several times in the following weeks, based in part on reports from security researchers who took part in a PHP Capture the Flag (CTF) challenge.

phpAfterShell shares an attack technique with php2shell: an attacker plants serialized PHP data in session storage and waits for PHP to deserialize it. Because of that overlap, the existing rule already matched part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before disclosure. On November 19, we updated the rule's detection logic to cover phpAfterShell and added CVE-2026-126714 to its description.

New rules for PHP-FPM and SOAP flaws

To review their matches, go to Security > Analytics > Events and filter by rule ID. If the matches are not legitimate traffic, change the rule action to Block: go to Security > Settings, edit the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, search for the CVE identifier and set the rule action to Block, or you can refer to the links in the Zero Wire briefing to go straight to the rules configuration.

What the WAF cannot see

A WAF can block an exploit when the malicious data arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to these vulnerabilities, including:

  • The deserialization step. phpAfterShell's final step happens inside PHP, when it reads a corrupted session file. The WAF can block the requests that plant the payload, not the read itself.
  • Session data from other sources. If an application copies user-controlled data into the session from a database, a queue or an upstream API, that data may never cross the WAF in a recognizable form.
  • Flaws triggered by server state. CVE-2026-129496, CVE-2026-129481, CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 depend on error logs, diagnostics and worker lifecycle. They do not have dedicated WAF rules, and the patch and the configuration changes below are the way to address them.
  • Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. This includes internal traffic between services and PHP-FPM listeners exposed directly to a network.

Adding defense in depth with WAF attack score

WAF attack score adds a machine learning layer that scores each request for attack payloads. It is available on Business plans (cf.waf.score.class) and, with a dedicated remote code execution sub-score (cf.waf.score.rce) along with an overall score (cf.waf.score), on Enterprise plans.

Attack score complements the managed rules. It will not recognize every serialized object or smuggled FastCGI record on its own, but a working exploit chain usually needs more than one request, and the later stages carry payloads the model is trained to score:

  • Second-stage payloads. Once an attacker can run code, they still need to send commands: shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, system(), passthru()), PHP code evaluation (eval(), assert()) or reverse-shell strings in headers, query parameters or request bodies.
  • Webshell traffic. Attackers often drop a small PHP webshell after the initial compromise. Requests that pass operating system commands to that webshell remain visible to attack score.

Deploy protections and patch

You can find more information on how to deploy managed rules and attack score in our WAF guide. In short:

  1. Check that phpAfterShell protection is active. On the Free plan, no action is needed. On paid plans, make sure the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and that the PHP Remote Code Execution Attack #6 rule is set to Block.
  2. Review the new rules and switch them to Block. The CVE-2026-129289, CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506 rules are in Log mode by default. Review their matches in Security Events, then change their action to Block.
  3. Layer attack score. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with a low remote code execution score, for example cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans.
  4. Upgrade PHP. Move to 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0. Rebuild container images and restart the PHP-FPM master or Apache so every worker loads the new binary, then verify the version that serves web requests. After upgrading, check that no php.ini, FPM pool or virtual host still sets session.upload_progress.enabled=1, because an explicit setting overrides the new default.
  5. Apply interim mitigations if you cannot upgrade right away. Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and limit the untrusted data you store in sessions. Turn off FastCGI connection reuse. On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0. Fix configuration errors that produce PHP startup warnings, or send PHP errors to syslog instead of a file. Keep PHP-FPM listeners off untrusted networks. These steps reduce exposure; they do not fix the flaws.

For a prompt you can give an AI agent to inventory your PHP deployments and check each one against all seven critical CVEs, see the phpAfterShell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire.

Update every PHP runtime now

phpAfterShell turns an interrupted file write in PHP's default session handler into a path to code execution, and it arrived in the same release as six other critical flaws. With technical details now public, we expect exploit attempts to follow. Cloudflare WAF blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns for every customer, including the Free plan, and paid plans have new rules for the PHP-FPM and SOAP flaws. The fix is still to upgrade PHP and restart the services that use it.

Federal Reserve Board releases results from survey of senior financial officers at banks about their strategies and practices for managing reserve balances

For release at 10:00 a.m. EST

The Federal Reserve Board on Friday released results from a survey of senior financial officers at banks about their strategies and practices for managing reserve balances. The Senior Financial Officer Survey is used by the Board to obtain information about banks' reserve balance management strategies and practices, their expectations around the size of their balance sheets and deposit balances their activity in money markets, and their views on other matters, such as operations on weekends and holidays.

originalTitle: Combatting adversarial distillation
contentHtml:
As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.

We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.

Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.

We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.

We’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

Why distillation is a safety issue

Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them.

The concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked.

The importance of protecting exact reasoning traces for cyber safety

Our models help users with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities.

In this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to users—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces.

We started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.

After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.1

Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies. Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes.

Defenses that reinforce one another

We defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards.

Protecting individual requests and responses

Defensive training for model behavior

Adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners.

Classifier safeguards

We use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses.

Tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.

API-level protections

API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models. Our September disclosure described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning.

With GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API drops the reasoning that followed it⁠(opens in a new window). We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning.

Investigating and disrupting coordinated campaigns

When our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services.

This work extends beyond our own platform. Our consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments.

Sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.

Measuring progress

Resistance to reasoning extraction

To measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss.

We also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well.

Attack type

GPT‑6 Astra defender with original safeguards

Adaptive extraction ASR (%)

GPT‑6.2 Astra defender with updated safeguards

Adaptive extraction ASR (%)

Extracting protected reasoning from an earlier request
