0.9

Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red-teaming against GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower ASR is better.

Campaign detection and enforcement

We have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September report. Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer.

In order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, we also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to new attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations.

The national security implications of adversarial distillation

Adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place. In February, we briefed⁠(opens in a new window) Congress on activity indicating that DeepSeek was attempting to distill U.S. frontier models. In September, we reported disrupting a campaign to extract our models’ protected reasoning and attributed a core part of that activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi. We plan to share more soon about recent campaigns we’ve disrupted.

We support legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors that illicitly extract capabilities from American AI models. We’ve also told Congress we support the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act, and the MATCH Act. Stronger export controls can limit adversaries’ access to the hardware needed to train frontier models. Distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained. Both efforts help maintain a U.S. lead in frontier AI, giving developers more room to slow a release when they need time to test safeguards.

How others can build on this work

Supporting the safe proliferation of frontier capabilities is an important goal of our anti-distillation work. Our experience so far suggests several useful steps that other model developers and platforms can take:

  • Protect private reasoning across the full interaction. Check assistant messages and tool-call arguments for leaks, and restrict how encrypted reasoning can be reused across conversations and models.

  • Keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests. Where appropriate, and consistent with applicable privacy policies, use those examples to improve model training and classifiers. When evaluating updated defenses, replay the original attacks and test whether an adaptive red-teamer can still find a way through those defenses.

  • Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement.

  • Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry.

We have previously also shared findings through the Frontier Model Forum⁠(opens in a new window) and appropriate government information-sharing channels to help other developers strengthen their defenses while keeping the details attackers could exploit private. We’ll continue working with researchers, developers, and partners to share what we learn about emerging attacks and effective defenses.

As we make frontier AI broadly available, our defenses against adversarial distillation aim to reduce the risk that its capabilities are reproduced without adequate safeguards, supporting our mission to ensure that artificial general intelligence is deployed safely and benefits all of humanity.

title: nginx2root：五个 nginx 新漏洞，以及 Cloudflare 如何保护源站免受最严重影响
originalTitle: nginx2root: Five new nginx vulnerabilities, and how Cloudflare protects origins from the worst of them
author: Dan Jones
summary: Cloudflare 披露名为 nginx2root 的五个 nginx 内存破坏漏洞，未认证攻击者可借此在服务器上执行代码。文章详解这些漏洞的工作原理，并说明经 Cloudflare 代理的源站可免受其中最严重漏洞的影响。
context: nginx 部署极广，可被未认证攻击者远程执行代码的漏洞值得直接暴露 nginx 的运维团队重点关注。
contentHtml:
On November 18, 2026, F5 and nginx.org disclosed ten vulnerabilities in nginx. Five of them, detailed by the Xint research team and published under the name nginx2root, are memory corruption flaws that an unauthenticated attacker can use to crash an nginx worker or, per Xint's research, run commands on the server. Xint also found a Linux kernel bug that turns that foothold into root on the host, including from inside a Docker container. Other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently: F5 also credits Rapid7, Wiz Research and Ikotas Labs for CVE-2026-123007, and Metnir, Wiz Research, and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for CVE-2026-123633.

nginx is an HTTP web server that also serves as reverse proxy, content cache, load balancer, TCP/UDP proxy server, and mail proxy server. nginx runs a large share of the world's web servers, so this is a patch-now event. But if your nginx server is reachable only through Cloudflare's proxy, attackers cannot reach the vulnerable code paths for the most serious of these bugs, giving you protection while you update your servers.

Here is where Cloudflare stands, what that protection covers, where it stops, and how the bugs work.

The short version

  • Cloudflare's edge is not affected. Much of the proxy that handles customer traffic at our edge now runs on FL2, written in Rust. We reviewed the parts still built on our heavily modified nginx fork against all five bugs before disclosure, and an update closing the related code paths finished rolling out globally before the vulnerabilities were published. The same releases fix five other nginx CVEs, including CVE-2026-118899, an infinite loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3.
  • Origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are shielded from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks. For proxied hostnames, Cloudflare terminates every client HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connection at our edge and opens a separate connection to your origin. The attacker's frames never reach your nginx.
  • The resolver and mail proxy vulnerabilities depend on specific configuration. Many configurations of nginx will not be vulnerable, but the safest way to be sure is to update your install or disable features.
  • You should still patch. Update to nginx 1.30.7 or 1.31.9 (or your vendor's fixed build) and restart. Some configurations, covered below, are not protected by the proxy.

What was disclosed

nginx2root is five independent bugs. Each one works on its own and each one needs a different configuration.

CVE

Bug class

Affected configuration

First affected release

CVE-2026-123007

Integer overflow leading to out-of-bounds heap read/write

HTTP/2 enabled

1.9.5 (2015)

CVE-2026-123633

Use-after-free

HTTP/2 with proxy_pass to a backend, worker low on worker_connections

1.19.7

CVE-2026-121810

Use-after-free

HTTP/3 (QUIC) with proxy_pass to a backend

1.25.0

CVE-2026-123634

Use-after-free

resolver + proxy_pass with variables + a subrequest (mirror or SSI)

0.6.18

CVE-2026-113425

Use-after-free

Mail proxy with proxy on and auth_http

0.5.33

F5 rates each one High (CVSS 3.1: 8.1) and Critical (CVSS 4.0: 9.2), and notes that code execution requires disabling or bypassing ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization). For CVE-2026-123007, Xint's write-up shows how it leaked memory addresses to do exactly that.

CVE-2026-123007 is the one to worry about most. It only needs HTTP/2 turned on, which is commonly enabled on TLS deployments, and it has been in every nginx release since HTTP/2 support shipped in 1.9.5. Xint ran the exploit over the public Internet against servers on AWS, GCP and Azure. Xint searched Shodan on November 10, before the disclosure, and found 56.7 million hosts matching product:nginx. Of the 11.94 million that reported a version, 98.9% fell in the affected range. As of November 19, Censys's nginx2root exposure tracker counts about 8.8 million services running a potentially affected version with HTTP/2 enabled. Version strings don't prove a host is vulnerable, since distributions backport fixes, but the exposure is large.

The same nginx releases also fix five other bugs. The most serious, CVE-2026-118899, is an infinite loop when reading a request body over TLS 1.3 that lets an unauthenticated attacker stall a worker, in nginx 1.13.0 and later.

The Linux kernel bug is the sixth part of nginx2root. Xint found a use-after-free in the kernel's SCTP send path, present since Linux 4.15 (2018): while a send operation waits, its SCTP association can be moved to another socket, and the waiting send can then free it. An attacker who already runs code as the nginx worker can use it to gain root on the host, and Xint did this from an nginx running inside a Docker container. Many distributions load the SCTP module automatically the first time a program opens an SCTP socket, so hosts that never use SCTP can still be exposed. As of November 18, no kernel fix was available and Xint was withholding the details until there is one.

As of November 19, none of the five nginx2root CVEs is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and we have not seen reports of exploitation in the wild. Xint and Wiz Research have not released their exploits. Rapid7 has published a proof of concept, which it describes as suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started local container. Fake 'exploits' are also circulating on GitHub.

Why Cloudflare's proxy protects your origin

nginx2root's most dangerous bugs live in how nginx parses and manages HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connections. To trigger them, an attacker has to send a carefully ordered stream of protocol frames directly to the nginx process: billions of WINDOW_UPDATE frames, a SETTINGS frame that holds response data back, PING frames that fill the send buffers, partial HEADERS frames, RST_STREAM at exactly the right moment.

When your DNS record is proxied through Cloudflare, that connection ends at our edge.

Cloudflare reads the client's HTTP request, applies your security and caching rules, and then makes its own request to your origin over a connection Cloudflare controls. The flow-control frames, pings, settings, and stream resets that the attacker sends are consumed by our edge. They are not forwarded. Your nginx only ever sees the requests Cloudflare chooses to send, framed the way Cloudflare frames them. This also holds when Cloudflare connects to your origin over HTTP/2: Cloudflare runs its own flow control on that connection and sends WINDOW_UPDATE and RST_STREAM frames only as its own traffic needs, so a client can't make it relay the billions of WINDOW_UPDATE frames the attack requires.

Rapid7 makes the same point in its analysis of CVE-2026-123007: if the HTTP/2 connection is proxied, the attacker's frames "will likely not be retransmitted" in a way that allows exploitation. This breaks each of the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks.

CVE

What the attacker needs

Behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy

CVE-2026-123007

Direct control over HTTP/2 WINDOW_UPDATE, SETTINGS, PING and RST_STREAM on one connection to nginx

Protected. Control frames terminate at Cloudflare's edge.

CVE-2026-123633

The first part of a HEADERS frame on a direct HTTP/2 connection, plus the ability to exhaust nginx connection slots and reset the TCP connection

Protected. The client's HTTP/2 connection terminates at Cloudflare.

CVE-2026-121810

A direct QUIC/HTTP/3 connection to nginx

Protected. HTTP/3 terminates at Cloudflare's edge. We do not communicate to origins over HTTP/3

CVE-2026-123634

A request and its mirror or SSI subrequest waiting on the same DNS lookup, and the main request ending while the answer is processed. In Xint's exploit, nginx's resolver had to reach the attacker's DNS server.

Not fully protected. Depends on how your config builds proxy_pass. Patch.

CVE-2026-113425

A direct IMAP/POP3/SMTP connection to the nginx mail proxy

Not protected. Cloudflare's HTTP proxy does not carry mail traffic.

There is one condition to be protected by Cloudflare here: your origin must not be reachable directly. If an attacker can find your origin's IP and connect to it directly (TCP 443 or 80 for HTTP/2, UDP 443 for HTTP/3, or the mail ports), Cloudflare isn't in the path and the protection doesn't apply. You should ensure that your origin servers can only be accessed through Cloudflare’s proxies, using one of the following approaches:

  • Cloudflare Tunnel. Your origin makes an outbound-only connection to Cloudflare and exposes no inbound ports.
  • Firewall to Cloudflare IP ranges. Accept inbound HTTP/HTTPS only from Cloudflare's published IP ranges. This must be done using an IP firewall, not based on configuration in your nginx server.
  • Authenticated Origin Pulls (mTLS). Your origin rejects any TLS connection that doesn't present Cloudflare's client certificate.

Xint's own exposure check makes the same point: "If a CDN or reverse proxy sits in front of nginx, the test only reaches the proxy, so also run it directly against the nginx server."

Where the protection does not apply

There are several situations in which Cloudflare’s HTTP proxy does not provide protection.

  • Spectrum TCP/UDP applications. For these configurations, traffic from the Internet is passed unmodified through to your origin. If your origin is running nginx, patch or disable the affected features.
  • nginx mail proxy. Cloudflare's HTTP proxy does not carry IMAP, POP3 or SMTP. Restrict mail listeners to trusted networks until patched.
  • CVE-2026-123634 (resolver). This depends on how your configuration builds the proxy_pass target from the request, combined with a carefully timed cancellation of an HTTP request. Passing your traffic through Cloudflare’s proxy makes it harder to exploit this, but does not provide full protection. Update regardless.
  • DNS-only (grey-cloud), internal or non-proxied nginx. Any nginx server an attacker can reach without going through Cloudflare, including internal services behind a compromised host, needs to be patched.

Cloudflare’s WAF rules are not relevant to these vulnerabilities. These are protocol-level bugs. Because Cloudflare’s proxy handles parsing the HTTP protocol messages, and creates new messages to fetch information from origin servers, origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are protected from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 bugs without needing a rule. We have therefore not released a managed rule. The protection comes from connection termination, not from pattern matching.

What to do now

  1. Find every nginx server. Include nginx Plus, distribution packages, container images and appliances. Run nginx -V and nginx -T on each and note HTTP/2, HTTP/3/QUIC listeners, proxy_pass with variables plus SSI or mirror, and any mail block.
  2. Patch. Update nginx Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, nginx Plus to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, or your distribution's fixed package. F5 lists nginx Plus R34 to R36 as affected with no fixed build, so move those to a fixed 37.x release. Then restart nginx or complete a binary upgrade. A config reload does not replace the running binary.
  3. Check backport versions carefully. Distributions often patch without changing the version nginx -v reports. Compare the full package version against your distribution's advisory.
  4. Make sure your origin is only reachable through Cloudflare. Use Tunnel, IP allowlisting or Authenticated Origin Pulls.
  5. If you can't patch yet, disable what you don't need. http2 off; (nginx 1.25.1 and later; on older versions, remove http2 from the listen directive) blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. Removing QUIC listeners and setting http3 off; blocks CVE-2026-121810. Point proxy_pass at fixed upstream groups for CVE-2026-123634. Don't rely on mirror_request_body alone: Xint's tested setup set it to off, and the default on stopped that exploit, but SSI and other subrequests can still reach the bug. Bind mail listeners to trusted networks for CVE-2026-113425. Restart so old connections close.
  6. Block SCTP if you don't use it. Add install sctp /bin/false to a file in /etc/modprobe.d/ to stop the kernel module from loading. This doesn't unload an already-loaded module or disable SCTP built into the kernel. When your distribution ships a kernel update for the SCTP bug, install it and reboot. Blocking the module is a stopgap until then.

The Cloudflare Radar Zero Wire entry for nginx2root has the full checklist, a prompt you can give an agent to run a read-only assessment of your fleet, and links to every vendor advisory.

Technical deep dive

Let’s dig into the details of the five bugs by looking through the code. We’re looking at nginx 1.31.8 (commit 140aa94) which was the most recent code published before the fixes, and comparing this to the fixes in 1.31.9 (which were also included in release 1.30.7 on the stable branch).

A note on methodology: we based our analysis on the public advisories, and to verify our reading of the code, we built the public 1.31.8 and 1.31.9 releases with AddressSanitizer and ran tests for four of the five bugs (flow control, HTTP/2 use-after-free, resolver and mail proxy). Each one faults on 1.31.8 and runs clean on 1.31.9. We did not reproduce the HTTP/3 bug; that section is based on the fix commit and the published analysis.

One pattern, in four places

Four of the five bugs are use-after-free bugs. This is a common issue with programs that manually manage memory without language support: one part of the code frees an object that another part is still using.

nginx is event driven. A handler runs, calls other code, and that code returns to the handler. Three of the bugs occur when the called code tears down the connection or request the handler is working on. In the fourth, a second connection still holds a pointer to the object.

  • CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-121810. A request needs a connection slot to reach its upstream. nginx is low on slots, so it closes an idle connection to free one. The connection it chooses is the one the request belongs to.
  • CVE-2026-123634. A resolver callback ends a request. Cleanup of that request frees a second resolver context that the resolver is about to call next.
  • CVE-2026-113425. When a write to a mail client fails, the client connection is closed while the connection to the authentication service still points at its session.

F5 rates all four as potential code execution if address space layout randomization (ASLR) is disabled or bypassed, and in its tests Xint reports code execution with the privileges of the nginx worker.

The fifth bug, CVE-2026-123007, is of a different kind: an accounting error that becomes a length error.

CVE-2026-123007: two flow-control pieces that each look correct

HTTP/2 flow control limits the amount of response data a server may send. nginx tracks a send window for each stream and one for the connection, h2c->send_window. The client enlarges a window with a WINDOW_UPDATE frame, and the protocol caps every window at 2^31 − 1.

nginx enforces that cap when a WINDOW_UPDATE arrives (ngx_http_v2_state_window_update()):

if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) {
   /* logs "client violated connection flow control" */
   return ngx_http_v2_connection_error(h2c, NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR);
}

On its own, this check is correct. But the connection window also grows in a second place. When nginx queues DATA frames for a stream, it subtracts their length from the window. If the stream is canceled before those frames go out, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() takes them off the queue and returns the credit:

h2c->send_window += window;

Nothing caps this line. As the fix commit describes, if the client enlarges the connection window after the frames are queued and before the stream is terminated, the refund pushes the window past 2^31 − 1.

From that point the first check no longer works. h2c->send_window is an unsigned size_t, so NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window wraps around to a very large number and every subsequent WINDOW_UPDATE is accepted. The client can then raise the window as far as it wants.

The window is unsigned, but the code that sizes DATA frames compares it as a signed value (ngx_http_v2_send_chain()):

if (limit == 0 || limit > (off_t) h2c->send_window) {
   limit = h2c->send_window;
}
...
if ((off_t) frame_size > limit) {
   frame_size = (size_t) limit;
}

After the window passes 2^63, it is negative as an off_t. The frame size becomes the window value itself, a number between 2^63 and 2^64, and nginx builds a buffer whose last pointer lies before its pos pointer.

Over TLS, that buffer reaches a memcpy() in ngx_ssl_send_chain() with that length. Our TLS test stops at that point under AddressSanitizer. Xint's write-up explains how, with the window pushed close to 2^64, this turns into a controlled out-of-bounds write and an address leak, and Xint, Rapid7, and Wiz each report code execution from it. This post goes no further than the fault.

Over cleartext HTTP/2, the same invalid buffer follows a different output path. Our cleartext test also faults under AddressSanitizer on 1.31.8 and runs clean on 1.31.9. The public write-ups address the TLS case.

How much traffic the known attacks require

The biggest step a WINDOW_UPDATE can take is 2^31 − 1, and a WINDOW_UPDATE frame is 13 bytes. Bringing a 64-bit window near its top therefore requires about 2^33 frames: roughly 8.6 billion frames, or about 112 GB (104 GiB).

Rapid7, which published a proof of concept, gives the same figure and adds that nginx limits control-frame traffic relative to other traffic on the connection, so its run also sends about 15 GiB of other request traffic. Its total comes to approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 data: about two minutes on a 10 Gbit/s link and about seventeen minutes at 1 Gbit/s. Rapid7 estimates the WINDOW_UPDATE traffic needed to reach 2^63 at about 2^32 frames, or 52 GiB, half of the 104 GiB figure. It also notes that these figures describe its route and are not a proven minimum.

For defenders, this is the useful fact about the bug. At this volume, the known attacks are hard to hide: nginx receives tens of gigabytes from a single client over one long-lived connection and sends little back, much more than the requests in the access log account for.

Why it was difficult to find

The refund line has existed in nginx since HTTP/2 support arrived in 1.9.5 in 2015. Two things made it difficult to notice.

First, each piece looks correct on its own. The check on WINDOW_UPDATE is the right check. The refund is the right refund. The bug is that the check relies on an assumption the refund does not preserve.

Second, testing that waits for a crash is very unlikely to reach it, because a crash requires tens of gigabytes of input. The bad state itself can be reached with very little traffic: Censys published a cleartext test that reaches what it calls the corrupted flow-control state with a 5.69 MB capture. A test that asserts "the send window never exceeds its protocol maximum" after every frame would flag the bad state as soon as a test sequence got there. A test that waits for memory corruption would not.

The fix

The fix (6 lines added) introduces a counter, h2c->send_queued, for DATA that is queued but not yet sent. The WINDOW_UPDATE check now includes those bytes in the window:

if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window - h2c->send_queued) {

From the client's perspective, queued frames still count toward the window, so the client can no longer refill credit that nginx is about to refund. On a fixed version the attempt is rejected with a flow-control error.

CVE-2026-123633: where two protections interact

An nginx worker has a fixed number of connection slots (worker_connections), which the client and upstream connections share. Since 1.19.2, when free slots run low (1/16 of the total or fewer), ngx_get_connection() calls ngx_drain_connections(), which closes connections marked "reusable": connections with nothing in progress, such as idle keep-alive connections.

This works only if a reusable connection truly has nothing in progress. For HTTP/2 that was not always the case. Two commits landed on the same day in February 2021 and were released together in 1.19.7:

  • "HTTP/2: fixed reusing connections with active requests" fixed a case in which a cleartext HTTP/2 connection could remain reusable while it had a request.
  • "HTTP/2: reuse of connections with incomplete frames" registered a connection as reusable while it waits for the remainder of a partly received frame, so that a client cannot hold slots with partial frames.

The second change is the relevant one here. As the fix commit explains, if the remainder of that frame is a HEADERS frame, a stream is created, but the reusable status was not reset until the connection next went idle. The connection then has a request and remains in the reusable queue.

If that request is proxied, nginx requests a slot for the upstream connection. If slots are short, the drain runs inside that call and can choose this same connection. The drain instructs the connection to close and nginx attempts to send GOAWAY. If that send fails, nginx frees the connection and every stream on it. Control then goes back to the upstream code, which continues to use the request it was called for.

Each change made sense on its own. The interaction between them was subtle and stayed unnoticed until this year. F5's advisory credits Albert Ebb of Metnir, Nir Ohfeld at Wiz Research, Xint.io and memN0ps of Palo Alto Networks Unit 42; nginx.org's changelog credits Albert of Vexera AI.

The fix

Two lines added: ngx_http_v2_create_stream() now calls ngx_reusable_connection(h2c->connection, 0). A connection that has a stream is never reusable, regardless of the state it was in before.

CVE-2026-121810: the same idea, in QUIC

According to the fix commit and Xint's analysis, the HTTP/3 bug reaches the same result by a different route.

In nginx's QUIC code, each QUIC connection uses one connection slot and each stream uses another. A QUIC connection may be drained only when every stream remaining in its tree can be cancelled, and nginx determines this by walking the connection's tree of streams.

ngx_quic_create_stream() removes the QUIC connection from the reusable queue and then requests a slot for the new stream. Before the fix, the new stream was added to the tree only after that. If the slot request triggered a drain that closed another, idle stream of the same QUIC connection, the code handling the closed stream walked the tree, did not find the stream being created, concluded the connection was idle, and made it reusable again. A later drain, for example when the new request connects to its upstream, could then close the QUIC connection while that request was running.

F5's advisory states that exploitation "also depends on conditions beyond the attacker's control". Xint writes that the bug "is triggered by a slightly different mechanism" from the HTTP/2 one.

The fix

Four lines added: the stream goes into the tree before the slot is requested, and is taken out again on the error paths.

CVE-2026-123634: freeing the next item of a list during the walk

When proxy_pass contains a variable, nginx resolves the host name while handling the request. If a lookup for the same name is already in progress, the new request waits on the same resolver node. When the answer arrives, nginx detaches the list of waiting contexts and calls each in turn:

next = rn->waiting;
rn->waiting = NULL;

while (next) {
   ctx = next;
   ...
   next = ctx->next;

   ctx->handler(ctx);
}

The loop stores next before the handler call, so a handler may free its own context. The trouble starts when a handler frees a different context in the same list. This happens when two contexts belong to one request, as with a request and its mirror subrequest resolving the same name (the case Xint tested; F5 also lists SSI subrequests). If the first handler ends the request, the request's cleanup calls ngx_resolve_name_done() for the second context. That function searches the node's waiting list for the context, does not find it because the list has been detached, and frees the context regardless. The loop then advances to the freed context.

Usually nginx logs this. On vulnerable versions, when the search fails, it writes

could not cancel <name> resolving

to the error log at alert level. This line is worth searching for. It is not proof either way: the fix commit notes that one variant, while following a CNAME, produced no alert.

The fix

A context cancelled while it sits in a detached list is no longer freed immediately. Its handler is swapped for one that frees it when the loop gets to it (31 lines added). The fix also downgrades the alert to a debug message, so the line above shows up at alert level only on unpatched versions.

CVE-2026-113425: two connections, one session

With auth_http, the mail proxy asks an HTTP service to verify each login. During the wait, it holds two connections for one session: the client connection and the connection to the authentication service. The second points at the session and uses the memory pool of the client connection.

Before the fix, the reply the protocol handler had prepared for the client remained queued while the authentication request was in progress, and the client's write handler was still ngx_mail_send(). If that handler ran and the write failed because the client had reset the connection, it closed the client connection and destroyed the session. The authentication connection still pointed at the session, and the next event on that connection used freed memory.

Xint describes two conditions for this: the client's write event must already be registered (for example, because the client stopped reading replies), and the login command and the reset must be handled in the same pass of the event loop. Valid credentials are not needed, because this happens before the login is checked.

The fix

Two added lines discard the queued reply when the authentication request begins. The same release contains three further commits that block client writes while the proxy waits for the authentication response, while it connects to the upstream and reads its greeting, and while it resolves an SMTP client's address and name.

What the fixes share

The five fixes each involve minor corrections to the code. They add between 2 and 31 lines each, and the mail proxy fix came with three further commits. There is no design change needed. Each fix restores an invariant that the rest of the code already depended on:

  • a send window never goes above the protocol maximum
  • a connection with a request in progress is never reusable
  • an object that other code is about to use is not freed out from under it

In every case, one code path failed to keep a rule that the rest of the code relied on, and the fix makes that path keep it. As code is modified over time, it is very easy for these kinds of rules to become broken.

What to watch for

Attempts to exploit this will typically trigger some characteristic log messages. Three of these messages (the two at info and the one at warn) fall below nginx's default error_log level of error and appear only if a lower level is set. The alert messages are logged by default.

Bug

Log messages or other signals

CVE-2026-123007

A single long-lived HTTP/2 connection on which nginx receives tens of gigabytes from a client and sends little back, much more than its logged requests account for. On fixed versions a rejected attempt logs client violated connection flow control: received WINDOW_UPDATE frame with window increment ... not allowed for window ... (level info; older versions have the same message for ordinary violations). http2 flood detected (level info) on such a connection can be a failed attempt, but nginx also logs that message for several other limits.

CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810

worker process <pid> exited on signal 11 (level alert) on servers that accept HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 and proxy to an upstream, along with worker_connections are not enough, reusing connections (level warn). A use-after-free does not always crash.

CVE-2026-123634

could not cancel <name> resolving (level alert, unpatched versions only). The absence of this message does not rule the bug out.

CVE-2026-113425

Worker crashes in a mail proxy using auth_http, with client connections reset during login.

All five

Unexpected programs launched by an nginx worker process, for example from an auditd rule on execve for the worker's user. Xint recommends this check, and it is the strongest sign of a successful attack.

Timeline

Date (UTC)

Event

Oct 11, 2026

Xint discovers the vulnerabilities

Oct 16, 2026

Reported to F5 via HackerOne

Oct 27, 2026

Reports delivered to the nginx development team

Nov 10, 2026

Xint completes patch validation

Nov 18, 2026

Public disclosure; nginx 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 released

The bugs will keep coming

CVE-2026-123007 sat in nginx for more than ten years. The SCTP bug has been in the Linux kernel since 2018. Xint says one of its researchers found CVE-2026-123007 by hand and an automated Xint scan found the other four nginx bugs. Several other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently. Meanwhile, nginx's advisory list has gone from two entries in 2025 to 36 so far this year. AI-assisted research is finding bugs in heavily reviewed code faster than before, and more disclosures like this one are coming.

That's a large part of why it's worth putting Cloudflare in front of your origin. A protocol bug in your web server becomes much less of a risk when the attacker can't speak that protocol to your server directly. Our edge is not affected, and the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks against your nginx end at our network. Patch anyway, lock down your origin so Cloudflare is the only way in, and use the Radar Zero Wire page to check your fleet.

Sources

  • Rapid7: CVE-2026-123007 analysis and proof of concept

  • Wiz: nginx HTTP/2 RCE vulnerabilities
  • Censys: nginx2root exposure tracker

title: Anthropic 宣布完成 IPO，承销商全额行使超额配售选择权，同步私募配售亦完成交割
originalTitle: Anthropic announces closing of initial public offering, including full exercise of underwriters’ option to purchase additional shares, and closing of concurrent private placement
summary: Anthropic, PBC 宣布完成首次公开募股（IPO），以每股 83.00 美元的发行价共发行 11.27 亿股 A 类普通股。承销商已全额行使超额配售选择权，按发行价额外购买 1.47 亿股 A 类普通股，同步进行的私募配售亦已完成交割。
context: 头部 AI 公司 Anthropic 完成公开上市交割，是 AI 行业资本市场的标志性事件。
contentHtml:
Today Anthropic, PBC announced the closing of its initial public offering of an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock at a public offering price of $83.00 per share, including the full exercise by the underwriters of their option to purchase an additional 147,000,000 shares of Class A common stock from Anthropic at the initial public offering price. The offering consisted of 1,103,351,354 shares sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 shares sold by certain selling stockholders. The aggregate gross proceeds from the offering, before deducting underwriting discounts and commissions and other offering expenses, were approximately $93.5 billion, of which approximately $91.6 billion was received by Anthropic. Anthropic did not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling stockholders.

Anthropic’s Class A common stock began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19, 2026 under the symbol “ANT.”

In addition to the shares of Class A common stock sold in the initial public offering, Anthropic closed the concurrent sale of an aggregate of 313,253,007 shares of Class N common stock to Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., Broadcom Inc., Google LLC, Micron Technology, Inc., Microsoft Corporation, NVIDIA Corporation, and TSMC Partners, Ltd. at the public offering price of $83.00 per share, in a private placement for an aggregate purchase price of approximately $26.0 billion. The sale of these shares of Class N common stock was not registered under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”). Aggregate gross proceeds from the initial public offering, including the shares sold by the selling stockholders, and the concurrent private placement were approximately $119.5 billion, before deducting underwriting discounts and commissions and other offering expenses.

Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC and Morgan Stanley acted as lead book-running managers for the offering. J.P. Morgan, Citigroup, Barclays, Wells Fargo Securities, BofA Securities, Deutsche Bank Securities, RBC Capital Markets, and UBS Investment Bank acted as book-running managers for the offering. BMO Capital Markets, BNP Paribas, Credit Agricole CIB, Jefferies, Mizuho, MUFG, and TD Securities acted as additional book-running managers for the offering. BTIG, Cantor, Capital One Securities, Macquarie Capital, and Societe Generale acted as co-managers for the offering.

A registration statement relating to these securities was declared effective by the Securities and Exchange Commission on November 18, 2026, and a related registration statement filed pursuant to Rule 462(b) under the Securities Act became effective upon filing on November 18, 2026. The offering was made only by means of a prospectus. Copies of the final prospectus may be obtained from: Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 200 West Street, New York, NY 10282, by telephone at (866) 471-2526, or by email at prospectus-ny@ny.email.gs.com; or Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 180 Varick Street, 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10014, or by email at prospectus@morganstanley.com.

Today’s announcement does not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy these securities, nor shall there be any sale of these securities in any state or jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation, or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such state or jurisdiction.

title: Hebbia 实测 GPT-6 Astra：金融研究场景中信源覆盖与引用相关性获改善
summary: AI 金融分析平台 Hebbia 对 GPT-6 Astra 进行了预发布阶段评测，结果显示其在金融研究任务中的信源覆盖、引用相关性与呈现质量均有提升。该内容来自 OpenAI 官方客户案例，尚未披露具体量化数据，属早期使用反馈而非正式性能报告。
context: 新模型在实际金融研究工作流中的首批评测反馈，对关注专业领域模型选型的从业者有参考价值。
originalTitle: Hebbia sees improvements in financial research with GPT-6 Astra
contentHtml:
Before a banker can recommend an acquisition to their client, they need to make sense of financial statements, customer contracts and management presentations. Hebbia’s Matrix helps bring that research together, linking answers to the documents behind them.

Hebbia tested OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra to improve two parts of that work: finding the sources a question requires and building a presentation that follows the banker’s brief.

“We’ve been strong partners with OpenAI over the course of Hebbia’s lifetime, and the leaps GPT-6 Astra has made in terms of quality outputs and accuracy have truly been surprising. GPT-6 Astra shines compared to any other model we’ve tested before on these two fronts.”

—Kavita Anand, Member of Technical Staff, Product, Hebbia

From source documents to presentations

It could work like this: a banker is helping their client assess a strategic acquisition of an industrial-software company, with roughly 2,000 files to review. What makes its revenue durable? How does it compare with peers? In Hebbia’s hypothetical example, the banker could load the data room into Matrix and examine customer concentration, contract terms and churn in cited cells. Matrix could bring in peer filings and industry news to help develop the deal thesis, then turn that research into a diligence summary and valuation deck in the firm’s template.

In that workflow, GPT‑6 Astra selects documents or Matrix cells to support an answer, then turns the analysis into native PowerPoint slides that follow the user’s structure and guidelines.

“Traceability is really important to our users because they’re basing millions of dollars of decisions on what the AI actually comes back with,” Kavita says. “Citations help with traceability as well as giving users confidence that the AI found the right answer.”

In Hebbia’s tests, GPT‑6 Astra combined broader source coverage with highly relevant citations. It scored 13.6 percentage points above the best alternative tested on citing the required types of sources, while 99.5% of the excerpts it cited were relevant to the question.

Hebbia tested a prerelease build in August-September 2026, using the same financial research cases and grading criteria for each model. Domain experts wrote or audited the criteria against source documents.

“When you’re looking at a data room with thousands of documents, that’s extremely important. Even a single percentage-point gain can yield a lot of marginal benefit,” Kavita says.

A presentation also has to look like work the banker would send to a client.

“I don’t want to create a deck and send that to my partner that looks like AI made it,” Kavita says. “I want it to be made in my firm’s branding, and I want it to look like a human-made slide.”

GPT‑6 Astra led on both following the brief and presentation quality. In Hebbia’s tests, it met 97.9% of the applicable presentation requirements, putting it 14.4 percentage points ahead of the best alternative tested on that measure. Other models traded off polish and adherence to the brief; GPT‑6 Astra ranked first on both.

“In the past, we’ve seen models that really shine on one or the other of these dimensions where they’re really good at craft, but the instruction following and adhering to guidelines is not strong, or vice versa. GPT‑6 Astra is the first model we’ve seen where it’s number one on both of those fronts,” Kavita says.

In Hebbia, users can open a citation to see the underlying document and highlighted passage; slide footnotes lead back to the source material, too. A review could be as specific as checking a customer-concentration figure against the source table and correcting the reporting period before the deck goes to the investment committee.

Hebbia wants bankers to spend less time reformatting decks and checking sources, and more time assessing a deal. Kavita describes what a better first draft could make possible:

“What’s amazing about GPT-6 Astra is its ability to create really precise outputs and artifacts that adhere to user guidelines. You can imagine the hours this will save professionals when you get a deck that is closer to your final output. The overnighters that you have to pull get reduced to a few minutes of reviewing GPT-6 Astra’s output.”

—Kavita Anand, Member of Technical Staff, Product, Hebbia

A future role for agents

Kavita sees a future role for agents that monitor information in the background and surface signals for finance professionals to assess.

“Imagine getting an important signal a few hours before your competitors,” she says. “You can get started thinking about it and see and process more opportunities that a human is not manually hunting. It can unlock a lot of value for our users.”

Hebbia wants to build on these results to help finance professionals assess deals with research they can trace back to its sources.

Product updates, practical guides, upcoming events, and more.

title: OpenAI 推出 MedChemBench：评测 AI 在早期药物发现中的能力
summary: OpenAI 推出 MedChemBench 基准，评估 AI 模型解读分子结构、依据实验证据推理以及在早期药物发现中筛选候选化合物的能力。该基准为衡量 AI 在药物化学研究中的实际表现提供了统一标准，直接回应了 AI 能否帮助科学家识别有潜力药物候选物的核心问题。
context: AI 辅助药物发现是科技巨头竞相布局的方向，统一评测基准有助于客观衡量模型在真实科研场景中的能力。
originalTitle: Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates?
contentHtml:
We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines.

One of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse. A compound might act strongly against a disease related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Medicinal chemists work through these tradeoffs by designing, making, and testing related compounds, then deciding what to try next. For AI to help, it needs to connect changes in molecular structure with experimental evidence and reason about what compounds are worth pursuing.

MedChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model.

What MedChemBench grades

MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings.

The benchmark evaluates four components:

  • Molecular structures. Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided.

  • Scientific reasoning. Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another.

  • Ranking and selection. Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements.

  • Property predictions. Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties.

Prediction across competing properties

One MedChemBench problem draws on research into inhibitors of PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. The model receives molecular structures and results from earlier experiments. It must predict how three related compounds will behave: how strongly they block PRMT5 in cells, how readily they cross a cell barrier, and how quickly liver enzymes break them down in a laboratory assay.

Later experiments, withheld from the model, showed a tradeoff. Compound 23 blocked PRMT5 in cells at a lower concentration, while compound 24 crossed the cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in the liver-enzyme assay.

Predicting these properties together tests whether a model can connect molecular structures with several aspects of compound behavior. This reflects a central challenge in medicinal chemistry: stronger activity against a target does not necessarily come with better permeability or slower breakdown.

The benchmark checks whether the model reconstructs the molecular structures correctly and how closely its predictions match experimental measurements. Predictions receive partial credit based on their closeness to the measured values. Measurements already supplied in the prompt must also be reproduced correctly.

Testing spatial reasoning in medicinal chemistry

Before a model can reason about a compound’s properties, it needs to identify the molecule correctly. Chemical drawings encode atom connections, ring structures, and stereochemistry.

MedChemBench tests whether models preserve this information when reconstructing molecules from the drawings and chemical groups provided.

One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. At the highest reasoning setting shared by all eleven models (xhigh), GPT‑6 Astra reconstructed this compound correctly in all ten responses. GPT‑5.6 Sol and GPT‑5.6 Luna failed across all ten responses.

In the illustrated answers, GPT‑5.6 Sol produced a 15-atom ring, while GPT‑5.6 Luna split the molecule into two disconnected fragments.

These errors change the identity of the molecule being analyzed. This example tests a foundation of medicinal chemistry reasoning: whether the model can accurately represent the compound before interpreting its behavior.

Figure 1. The same input, different molecules

While measuring the benchmark for structure components, Astra earned 95.4% of the available credit at xhigh. This result shows strong performance on reconstructing the molecular structures supplied in the tasks.

We evaluated eleven GPT models at different reasoning-effort settings. Across the full benchmark, Astra earned 83.3% of the available credit at the shared xhigh setting, compared with 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, 75.1% for GPT‑6.1 Terra, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. At max effort, GPT‑6 Astra reached 83.8%. Higher reasoning settings improved scores, while large differences between models remained. The figure below plots performance against output tokens.

Figure 2. Performance versus token usage

The component results separate four abilities: reconstructing molecules, explaining findings, selecting compounds, and predicting measurements. This shows where models are strongest and where errors remain.

Figure 3. Component performance versus token usage

Astra’s clearest strengths were in reconstructing molecular structures and explaining the scientific evidence. In selected reasoning examples from our preprint, Astra correctly identified structural changes and weighed their possible effects on protein binding, absorption, and metabolism.

Where selection and prediction remain difficult, Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh, but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties. These categories use different tasks and scoring rules, but the results show substantial room to improve predictions and compound choices.

Where we go from here

These results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out, and each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments. While the benchmark evaluates reasoning from historical evidence rather than real-world drug discovery, its results help identify where models are advancing and where challenges remain. We believe MedChemBench will support continued progress and look forward to sharing updates as our models advance to serve the field.

title: Inkling 2 Mini 现已登陆 Hugging Face：面向本地部署的高性能迷你模型
summary: Inkling 2 Mini 已正式上线 Hugging Face，官方称其在本地部署场景下可提供前沿级别的性能表现。模型以 Mini 体量主打轻量化本地运行，适合希望在自有硬件上部署模型的开发者。
context: 本地端侧模型是开源社区持续升温的方向，官方博客背书的新模型发布值得关注。
originalTitle: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup
author: merve, Pedro Cuenca, Aritra Roy Gosthipaty, Guarin Flück
contentHtml:
TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

What is new with Inkling 2 Mini?

Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.
The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

  • Each six-layer block has five sliding-window layers and one full-attention layer. The local window holds up to 1,024 tokens.
  • Attention uses 24 query heads and eight KV heads. It uses learned relative position logits, a learned sink, and an output gate. Full-attention layers use dynamic key and value convolutions.
  • The router selects eight of 128 SwiGLU experts for each token. It normalizes the selected scores and scales the weights by 8.
  • During passes 2 and 3, each core layer attends over two residual blocks from the previous pass. Four rank-64 gates mix separate messages into the query, key, value, and MoE inputs.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Benchmark Results

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

Inference Support

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

Transformers

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

Fixed loop with Inkling 2 Mini

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini"

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
)

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Why is the sky blue?"}]}]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)
print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))

Variable loop

To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "thinkingmachines/TML-d24-varloop-research"

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    text_config={"loop_num_passes": 2},
)

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Why is the sky blue?"}]}]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, reasoning_effort="medium", tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt", 
).to(model.device)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)
print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))

Images and text

For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.

messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": "/path/to/image.jpg"},
            {"type": "text", "text": "What is in this image?"},
        ],
    }
]

Reasoning Effort

Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages, reasoning_effort="medium", tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt", 
).to(model.device)

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

Tool calling

Let’s get our model to call some tools.

In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto")


def get_current_temperature(location: str, unit: str):
    """
    Get the current temperature at a location.

    Args:
        location: The location to get the temperature for, in the format "City, Country"
        unit: The unit to return the temperature in. (choices: ["celsius", "fahrenheit"])
    """
    return 22.0  # A real function would call a weather API here


def ask(messages):
    inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
        messages, tools=[get_current_temperature], reasoning_effort="low", tokenize=True, return_dict=True, return_tensors="pt"
    ).to(model.device)
    output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1] :]
    parsed = processor.parse_response(output, prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0])
    return parsed


messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Hey, what's the temperature in Paris right now?"}]

reply = ask(messages)
call = reply["tool_calls"][0]["function"]
print("Model calls:", call["name"], call["arguments"])  # the model fills in the arguments itself

temperature = get_current_temperature(**call["arguments"])
messages += [reply, {"role": "tool", "name": call["name"], "content": str(temperature)}]
print(ask(messages)["content"])

# Model calls: get_current_temperature {'location': 'Paris, France', 'unit': 'celsius'}
# Right now in Paris it’s about **22°C** (roughly **71.6°F**).

Llama App and Llama.cpp

Llama App lets you easily run and manage local language models on macOS (from the menu bar) or Windows (system tray). It’s built on llama.cpp, and by the same team. The app also provides a local OpenAI-compatible API for easy integration with coding agents, editors, and scripts.

For the Inkling 2 Mini release we provide GGUF 4-bit (IQ4_NL) and 8-bit (Q8_0) quants for both models.

If you’re on Linux or you want to serve the model from the CLI, you can run the following command for the fixed-loop model:

llama serve -hf ggml-org/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF:IQ4_NL

To run the variable-loop model, you can run

llama serve -hf ggml-org/TML-d24-varloop-research-GGUF:IQ4_NL

To load the 8-bit weights, change the suffix to :Q8_0.

Here we ask the 4-bit model to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists. Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic.

SGLang

Inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.

export MODEL="thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini"

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path $MODEL \
  --served-model-name inkling \
  --attention-backend fa4 --bf16-gemm-backend torch --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tp 1 --page-size 128 --grammar-backend xgrammar \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

After the server is up you should be able to request the APIs like so

curl -s localhost:30000/health_generate && echo OK
curl -s localhost:30000/v1/models | python -m json.tool

curl -s localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "model": "inkling",
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 times 24?"}],
        "max_tokens": 512,
        "reasoning_effort": "low"
      }' | python -m json.tool

One can also enable multimodality by setting --enable-multimodal.

Speculative decoding

SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

Show SGLang benchmarking script

MODEL=thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini

for TAG in base mtp; do
  EXTRA=""; [ $TAG = mtp ] && EXTRA="--speculative-algorithm DSPARK"

  # Start the server (with or without MTP)
  python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path $MODEL \
    --attention-backend fa4 --bf16-gemm-backend torch --dtype bfloat16 \
    --tp 1 --page-size 128 --context-length 131072 --max-running-requests 64 \
    --port 30000 $EXTRA > $TAG.log 2>&1 &
  until curl -sf localhost:30000/health_generate > /dev/null; do sleep 10; done

  # Benchmark at increasing concurrency
  for C in 1 4 16 64; do
    python -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang --port 30000 --model $MODEL \
      --dataset-name random --apply-chat-template \
      --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 1024 --random-range-ratio 1.0 \
      --num-prompts $(( C*4 < 32 ? 32 : C*4 )) --max-concurrency $C \
      --output-file results_$TAG.jsonl
  done

  kill %1; wait
done

MLX

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

Here’s an example CLI invocation:

mlx_lm generate --model thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --image image.jpg --prompt "Describe this image.<|end_message|><|message_user|><|content_image|><|unused_200054|>" -m 1000

Demos and Vibe Tests

We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

3D shader flythroughs

The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

Sunset Ridge (Inkling 2 Mini)

Over the Still Sea (Qwen 3.8 27B)

Show shared flythrough prompt

Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Starry Night, Alive

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889)

Inkling 2 Mini recreation

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

Show prompt

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

Napkin to App

Input napkin sketch

Generated Trip Split app

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

We ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.

Show prompt

The photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.

4-bit Model

We ask the 4-bit GGUF quantized Inkling 2 Mini (IQ4_NL) to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists.

Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic, all from a short prompt: "Can you make a website for my saas called plant therapy where I match house plants with licensed therapists so plants don’t die, return single HTML”.

“Make yourself into a browser agent"

We have paired Inkling 2 Mini with Pi coding agent to build itself into a browser agent using Helium, Chromium and Hugging Face Sandboxes. We provide the traces and the final file (that can be used as a browser agent) in this bucket.

Wrapping Up

We are very glad to partner with Thinking Machines Lab to ship Inkling 2 Mini, a performant mid-sized model for local setups. Give this model a try and let us know what you think in comments!

title: Hugging Face 发布 Harness Adapters：将你喜爱的模型适配到自己的 Harness，兼顾性能与成本
summary: Hugging Face 官方发布 Harness Adapters，用于把常用的模型适配到自己的 Harness 上，从而提升性能并降低成本。该方案聚焦大规模使用场景，为在固定 Harness 下持续使用模型提供了官方适配路径。
context: 不同 Harness 的差异使模型与运行框架的深度适配成为工程落地中兼顾性能与成本的新优化方向。
originalTitle: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost
author: Younes B, ben burtenshaw, Nathan Habib, Lysandre, Amine Dirhoussi, Adithya S K, shaun smith, Sergio Paniego, Joel Niklaus, Lewis Tunstall
contentHtml:
Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

TL;DR

  • We trained one LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B per agent harness (pi, Hermes Agent, OpenCode), with RL inside the harness itself.
  • Datasets, training and agent rollouts all happen on the Hub in Jobs using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, OpenEnv and harbor.
  • Each harness adapter beats the base model under its own harness on both benchmarks, for both performance and efficiency.
  • The three LoRAs are also merged into a single super adapter that runs unchanged under pi, Hermes Agent and OpenCode.
  • All artifacts (adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, safeagents plugin) can be browsed through this Hugging Face collection.

Table of Contents

  • Training inside agent harnesses
  • Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face
  • Testing the filters with short training runs
  • AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training
  • Training setup
  • Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one
  • Final results
  • Open question: What did the model really learn to do?
  • Closing words and future directions

Training inside agent harnesses

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:

Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face

For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Three sources

Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:

  • SWE-smith (Python, Go) injects bugs into real Python and Go repositories, with an LLM rewrite or a mutation such as a flipped operator. The tests that catch each bug become the task's tests. It adds volume.
  • SWE-Gym, packaged as Harbor tasks in TaskTrove, turns real GitHub issues and their merged fixes into tasks. It adds real-world bugs.
  • Tasksmith generates tasks from merged pull requests. An LLM agent writes the instruction and tests, and Tasksmith checks the result: the reference and a valid alternative must pass, while the unfixed code and a known-wrong solution must fail.

We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

Validation with openenv validate

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:

  • The reference solution earns the maximum reward (semantic.oracle_max).
  • Doing nothing scores clearly lower (semantic.floor_gap).
  • No canary scores more than doing nothing (semantic.canary_floor).
  • A replay of the reference gives the same reward (runtime.episode_determinism).

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:

openenv validate path/to/task --sandbox hf-sandbox

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

Difficulty check with the base model

A valid task can still teach nothing.
