GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

Testing the filters with short training runs

The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:

  • Unvalidated: 24 accepted tasks plus 8 that failed validation.
  • Validated: 32 accepted tasks, chosen without regard to difficulty.
  • Unqualified: 32 accepted tasks that the base model always or never solves.
  • Qualified: 32 accepted tasks that the base model solves on some attempts.

The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

The dataset

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

Source Task type Tasks Qualified
SWE-smith Injected bugs in Python and Go 717 144
SWE-Gym (TaskTrove) Real GitHub issues 130 27
Tasksmith Generated from merged pull requests 24 22
Total 871 171

AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

Training setup

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Training infrastructure

Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

Final mixture

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:

Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

safeagents in the loop

We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one

Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:

  • ⅓ (the average): each harness keeps only a third of its own update.
  • ½: each update at half strength.
  • 1 (the plain sum): every update applied in full.
Weight pi hermes opencode All three harnesses Tool calls per task
base model 39.1% 46.0% 44.8% 43.3% 49.2
⅓ (average) 49.4% 51.2% 47.1% 49.2% 35.6
½ 48.8% 53.5% 55.2% 52.5% 25.9
1 (sum) 40.2% 62.8% 47.1% 50.0% 13.4

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Adapter merging evaluation results

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):

Harness Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B Qwen3.8-27B-<harness>-adapted Qwen3.8-27B-super-adapter Qwen3.8-27B, thinking Qwen3.8-27B-super-adapter, thinking
pi SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 40.0% 64.0% (−60%) 46.0% (−73%) 74.0% 74.0% (−48%)
hermes SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 29.4% 43.1% (−56%) 47.1% (−60%) 45.1% 60.8% (−36%)
opencode SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 35.3% 51.0% (−72%) 45.1% (−63%) 47.1% 66.7% (−31%)
pi Terminal-Bench 2.1 40.0% 56.5% (−56%) 48.2% (−56%) 52.9% 57.6% (−25%)
hermes Terminal-Bench 2.1 44.7% 58.8% (−70%) 55.3% (−53%) 58.8% 63.5% (−19%)
opencode Terminal-Bench 2.1 47.6% 52.4% (−53%) 52.4% (−68%) 54.9% 58.5% (−22%)

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

Final results

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training results

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

Evaluation results

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

Evaluation setup

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

Final evaluation results

All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

Does the efficiency and performance ability transfer across harnesses?

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

Evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks and setup

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

Model pass@1 (all assertions met) vs base Partial credit (share of assertions met) vs base
base 23.0% 62.2%
pi 160 27.0% +4.0 66.2% +4.0
opencode 150 25.3% +2.3 65.2% +3.0
merged 23.7% +0.7 60.6% −1.6
hermes 160 17.7% −5.3 56.6% −5.6

Open question: What did the model really learn to do?

We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Closing words and future directions

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

title: 谷歌研究院发布博文：一款没有量子计算机就无法获胜的游戏
summary: 谷歌研究院发布博文，解析一款只有量子计算机参与者才能获胜的游戏，直观展示量子计算相对于经典计算的优势。文章以游戏形式说明量子计算机能在特定任务上完成经典方法无法实现的事情。这种互动式讲解降低了量子优势概念的理解门槛，对开发者与科普读者都有参考价值。
context: 量子优势的直观演示是理解近期量子计算价值的关键，顶级实验室的通俗解读具有行业科普意义。
originalTitle: A game you cannot win unless you have a quantum computer
contentHtml:
Here is a Sunday paper-style puzzle you can try right now. Draw a 3×3 grid. Fill every cell with either +1 or −1, subject to two rules: each row must multiply to +1, and each column must multiply to −1.

Go ahead. We’ll wait…

You didn’t manage it, right? There is an elegant reason for that. For a row to multiply to +1, it needs an even number of −1s. For a column to multiply to −1, it needs an odd number. Add up the rows and you learn the grid contains an even number of −1s. Add up the columns and you learn it contains an odd number. Well…That’s impossible!

The grid would have to be two contradictory things at once. No such table exists; it is a paradox.

Now turn the puzzle into a game: Each round, Alice is handed a row and Bob a column. Without talking, Alice fills her row by the row rule and Bob fills his column by the column rule. They win if they put the same number in the square where their row and column intersect. Any plan made in advance is just a pre-written table, meaning at best they will win 8 out of 9 rounds. This changes if they use a quantum computer. It won't fill in the impossible grid, but in principle, it lets them win every round.

The reason is a property called quantum contextuality, arguably the strangest feature of quantum mechanics. Einstein once famously asked whether the moon is there when nobody looks, his way of insisting that physical properties ought to exist whether or not anyone measures them. For quantum systems, contextuality is the precise, experimentally testable statement that the answer can be no: you cannot assign fixed, pre-existing values to everything you might measure.

What a measurement yields can depend on which other compatible measurements you make alongside it (i.e., on its context). This is not only a deep philosophical statement, but more so, cutting-edge science and the basis of a new technology. And in the game above, Alice and Bob can use it to engineer a solution. Their answers are not looked up in a hidden table written in advance; the table does not exist. Their answers come into being as they measure, and quantum correlations stitch them together more tightly than any classical rulebook permits.

Entanglement usually gets top billing as the “magic ingredient” of quantum computing. But a growing body of theory suggests contextuality is the deeper resource, the thing that actually powers certain quantum algorithms past their classical counterparts. The catch is that, until recently, contextuality had been demonstrated almost exclusively in small systems of a few particles. Whether it survives, and stays useful, in the many-body systems that real quantum computers are made of was an open question.

That is the question we set out to answer. In "Quantum-classical separation in bounded-resource tasks arising from measurement contextuality," published in Science, we demonstrate and measure contextuality on our superconducting quantum processors. Our qubits win the magic square game 98.3% of the time, exceed the classical limit on a contextuality test, and outperform classical strategies in tasks spanning up to 105 qubits. Along the way, these tasks proved to be a sensitive new benchmark for quantum hardware, catching subtle errors that random-circuit tests miss.

Beating the classical bound

We ran what is commonly called the magic square game on our Willow quantum processor. Alice and Bob each hold two qubits, sharing two entangled Bell pairs instead of a pre-written table, and measure them using preset settings for their assigned row or column to get their ±1 entries.

The best conceivable classical strategy loses at least one round in nine, winning at most 88.89% of the time. When we played all nine versions of the game 100,000 times apiece, our qubits lost roughly one in sixty, winning 98.30% of them (0.9830 ± 0.0001).

The gap is meaningful and statistically significant: our qubits coordinated better than any pre-written table allows. That's because no cell has a value fixed in advance. Each answer takes shape only when it is measured alongside the rest of its row or column (its context), and shared entanglement makes Alice's and Bob's answers for the shared cell agree.

Putting a number on contextuality

The magic square game demonstrated the potential power of contextuality, so next we set out to measure how contextual a machine is. We used a Bell–Kochen–Specker inequality, closely related to the famous Bell test which showed that entangled particles like the Bell pairs above can't carry answers fixed in advance. Our inequality bundles a set of correlations into a single number, χ. In terms of the rows and columns from the game above it reads, χ = R1 + R2 + R3 − C1 − C2 − C3, where R and C represent the products of the rows and columns Alice and Bob had to calculate earlier:

+1 +1 +1 R1 = (+1)*(+1)*(+1) = +1
+1 −1 −1 R2 = (+1)*(−1)*(−1) = +1
−1 +1 −1 R3 = (−1)*(+1)*(−1) = +1
C1 = (+1)*(+1)*(−1) = −1 C2 = (+1)*(−1)*(+1) = −1 C3 = (+1)*(−1)*(−1) = +1 χ = 4

Any universe where measurement outcomes are predetermined must obey χ ≤ 4 (try a few tables and you will see that χ can only take values -4, 0, and 4). Quantum mechanics permits values up to 6, which can only happen if all Rs = +1 and all Cs = -1. And unlike most such tests, this one is state-independent: it doesn’t matter how you prepare the qubits, which makes it a property of the machine rather than of a carefully chosen input.

Measuring χ is demanding: every row and column must be measured on the same two qubits, one after another, without disturbing them. We did this with an extra helper qubit (an "ancilla") that picks up each result and is measured instead, leaving the two main qubits intact. We ran 540 measurements in a row, repeated 1,000 times.

We measured χ = 5.590 ± 0.008.

Comfortably past the classical bound of 4 and only 7% away from the quantum limit. A number that says: the contextuality is in this machine in this quantity.

Does it survive at scale?

Two qubits are one thing, but quantum effects are fragile, and every added qubit brings noise that can wash them out. Useful quantum computing needs many qubits working together, so the question is whether contextuality survives at scale.

In the GHZ parity game, N players share one entangled GHZ state (a superposition of all qubits being 0 and all being 1). Each player gets a one-bit question and answers with one bit, without communicating. They win if the parity (even or odd) of all the answers matches a rule set by the questions. Random guessing wins half the time, and the best classical plan does only a bit better: 75% for three players, shrinking toward 50% as players are added. A shared GHZ state wins every time. We played with up to 71 players, one per qubit. Noise keeps us below 100% and grows with each added qubit, so our lead narrows, but we stay above the classical bound throughout. We also verified genuine entanglement across 45 qubits, more than the full size of many earlier GHZ experiments.

Beyond multiplayer games, the same physics separates shallow quantum and classical circuits. In 2018, a landmark theorem proved that a specific problem, finding a hidden linear function, can be solved by a constant depth quantum circuit, and that no classical circuit of constant depth can. The source of this quantum advantage traces back to contextuality.

In this proof, constant depth matters. It means the circuit doesn’t get deeper as the problem gets bigger. Because every output bit is computed in a fixed number of steps, information has time to travel only a short distance. Each classical output can therefore only “see” a small neighborhood of the input, like a rumor that must cross a city in three minutes. Quantum circuits, with entanglement already laid down, are not so limited.

That algorithm had never been run at scale on real hardware. We ran it, solving hidden-linear-function instances on grids of up to 105 qubits, with success probabilities above one-half, using exactly the shallow-circuit recipe the theory prescribes.

The unexpected dividend: A better ruler

While running these experiments, something useful happened along the way. These tasks demand that many qubits agree simultaneously and exactly. Running them surfaced subtle coherent errors in our system, the kind that rotates a quantum state slightly off-target, which conventional random-circuit benchmarks tend to average away into invisibility.

That suggests a second use for contextuality: not just as a computational resource, but as a ruler.

Most benchmarks ask whether a processor can clear some classical bar. These tasks instead give hardware a ceiling set by physics itself: χ = 6, a win probability of 1, a perfect contextual fraction. The distance between what a machine achieves and what nature permits becomes an objective, meaningful score. And unlike classical bars that get easier to clear, this ceiling never moves. The better our quantum processors get, the more precisely such a benchmark discriminates. This is particularly relevant for real-world applications, such as simulations of molecules for chemistry and materials science, because it measures a processor’s ability to run structured algorithms, where subtle errors can’t hide.

What comes next

A nearly century-old argument about whether physical systems always exist when nobody looks turns out to have a measurable test. For our qubits, the verdict is clear: not everything we measure can have pre-existing values waiting to be observed. Theory links contextuality to the "magic states" that error-corrected quantum computers need to run full algorithms, which our team recently prepared using magic state cultivation.

Measuring contextuality across many qubits lets us probe an open question in physics and computer science on real hardware: what gives quantum computers their edge.

Acknowledgements

This work was carried out by the Google Quantum AI team together with our academic collaborators. We thank everyone who built and maintained the hardware, control electronics, cryogenics and software that made these experiments possible.

title: NVIDIA 展示开发者如何用前沿 AI 智能体在 Omniverse 中构建仿真应用
summary: NVIDIA 官方博客介绍开发者将前沿 AI 模型与 Omniverse 库结合，把仿真构想转化为可运行应用的工作方式。该流程涵盖组装资产、连接物理与渲染、验证场景行为，应用于场景探索、故障排查和设计改进。
context: 展示了 AI 智能体在工业仿真开发中的实际落地路径，对从事数字孪生与仿真工具开发的工程师有参考价值。
originalTitle: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
author: NVIDIA Writers
contentHtml:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.

Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.

Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.

Physical AI Paves the Path to Autonomous Industrial Operations 🔗

AI agents powered by frontier models pave the way to autonomous operations. They use industrial tools and engineering data to help engineers build digital twins that test plans and processes and evaluate operational decisions.

Falkor, a KONGSBERG company, shows how this works in practice. The company’s Falkor Surface platform lets customers turn their computer-aided design and engineering data into facility-scale digital twins using the GPT-6 Astra model. The platform uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition GPUs on Microsoft Azure to enable advanced physics simulation.

AI agents built on Falkor’s agentic engine understand dense technical documentation, spatial relationships and real-world physics. Engineers can create and test plans in simulation before traveling on site, reducing costly delays and mistakes. They can also inspect equipment and check clearances in a shared view.

Read Falkor’s article and watch the livestream for a closer look at how the company builds these tools and checks the agents’ work.

Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗

Getting a robot model into a scene is only the start. Developers also need to assemble its components, add controls and check whether it can complete a task.

NVIDIA developers Dillon Bailey and Rishabh Chadha used 3D assets from the SimReady Central library to build a pick-and-place simulation of a robot moving a can using the NVIDIA Isaac Sim framework. They directed an agent equipped with GPT-6 Sol and Isaac Sim skills to assemble the scene and generate pick-and-place controls.

Testing the assembled scene shows how the assets work together, from joint movement and contact behavior to the gripper’s ability to hold, move and release the can. With that baseline in place, developers can adjust object positions and motion paths and repeat the tests to evaluate how each change affects the task.

Follow the walkthrough to assemble and test a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim, with sample agent prompts and checks for robot movement and grasp behavior.

Build a Voice-Controlled VR Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗

Bringing 3D assets into virtual reality (VR) requires more than rendering a scene. Objects need to respond to controllers and behave as expected when grabbed, moved or released.

NVIDIA Omniverse community developer Michael Wagner took on this challenge. He directed GPT-6 Astra to use Blender software to model a study environment from two reference images, balancing visual quality with efficient performance in VR. 

He then used Claude Code to build an application that lets users find SimReady Central assets by voice and interact with them in an immersive VR scene. The Claude Code agent worked for about eight hours, and Wagner built the application over a weekend using an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada workstation and a Meta Quest 3 VR headset. 

The application ran on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries: ovstage shared the OpenUSD scene, ovrtx rendered it, ovxr enabled VR and ovphysx ran physics. Wagner later built a second version with ovnewton, which integrates with ovstage, to compare the physics libraries.

The biggest challenge for Wagner was checking what happened inside the headset. Automated tests missed problems he could feel, including objects shaking when grabbed. Wagner reported the symptoms, guided the agent through changes and verified the interaction himself. Updating the grab control once per frame resolved the shaking. His takeaway: Give agents renders and logs to inspect, then check the experience directly. 

Explore his open source demo for build instructions, a starting prompt and reusable agent skills.

Send Microducks on Rounds in a Simulated Hospital 🔗

Before adapting a robot to a new environment, developers need to test whether its walking policy — the AI that controls how it moves — can keep it stable in that setting.

AI developer Maziyar Panahi directed Claude Code, using Claude Opus 5.5, to assemble an intensive care unit from 13 NVIDIA SimReady hospital assets and test Microduck robots inside it. The assets came with Newton physics settings, so Panahi didn’t have to model the furniture or create collision geometry from scratch. The Newton physics engine also helped replicate the ward so hundreds of copies could run together on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU.

When the cloud containers lacked graphics support, Panahi and the Claude Code agent separated simulation from rendering, recording robot poses in the cloud and rendering them locally. They also treated the furniture as static collision objects, which enabled larger runs within the solver’s limits. 

The robots walked using AI they had already been trained on and followed preset points along a route. Panahi checked how many robots remained upright: In a 256-ward run, 766 of 768 Microducks were still standing after 14 simulated seconds. He said the agent’s work took about two hours.

Explore the open source demo for a starter prompt, checks and instructions to begin with one ward on a CPU, then scale to hundreds on an NVIDIA GPU.

Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents 🔗

Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance.

In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering.

Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training.

Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools.

These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications.

Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill.

Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗

Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.

Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation.

PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model.

Read Sensori’s story.

Explore the Onshape importer guide.

Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗

Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation.

David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes.

Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection.

Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries.

Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗

Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator.

The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error.

The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing.

Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene (ovstage), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments.

Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗

With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin, developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows.

Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments.

For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment.

Find assets in SimReady Central Library, and learn how to contribute.

Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗

A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene.

When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns.

Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling.

With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements.

Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve.

Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.

Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗

In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit.

Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable.

Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments.

The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors.

Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab.

Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗

Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task.

Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.

Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot.

Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial. 

Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗

Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view.

Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views.

DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics (ovphysx), scene updates (ovstage), rendering (ovrtx) and the user interface (ovui). He also used Astra with SimReady (simready-foundation) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together.

Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.

Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗

Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street.

Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions.

Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗

Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene.

To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones.

Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement.

Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example, then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data.

Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗

Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements.

Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control.

Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.

Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗

Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible.

The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering (ovrtx), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections.

Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill.

Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗

A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio.

The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. 

Explore USD Content Agents.

Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.
